competitor_links.source_title: United Homes Group DEFM14C (filed 2026-04-10)

ma.counterparty: Holiday Builders, Inc. (Melbourne, FL; employee-owned)
ma.description: Agreement announced 16 July 2026 (Stanley Martin's website copy is dated 20 July). Holiday says the acquisition became official on 30 July 2026, and Holiday is now a wholly owned subsidiary. Price not disclosed. Holiday closed about 1,050 homes in 2025 and adds about 10,600 controlled Florida lots and 40+ communities. Zelman Partners advised Holiday, with Holland & Knight as counsel. Maynard Nexsen and Larry Eisenberg, PC acted for Stanley Martin.
ma.map_impact: Holiday (Builder 100 #62) merges into Stanley Martin (#18). Stanley Martin's Florida business grows from Orlando and Tampa to seven regional zones, from the Panhandle to the Southwest Gulf Coast. The 10,600 lots, mostly scattered and finished lots bought from developers, make Stanley Martin a much larger Florida lot buyer. Bruce Assam stays President and CEO of Holiday. Land decisions likely now involve Reston (inference).
ma.source_title: Stanley Martin Homes press release: Stanley Martin Homes to Acquire Holiday Builders (July 2026)
ma.note: Closing date from Holiday's own post of 2 Sep 2026 (https://holidaybuilders.com/holiday-builders-aquired-by-stanley-martin-homes/). The seller's adviser has reported 29 July. Daiwa lists the deal as July 2026 in its Integrated Report 2026, and its 11 Nov 2026 Q&A puts UHG plus Holiday at about 1,500 homes a year in FY2026.

ma.counterparty: United Homes Group, Inc. (Nasdaq: UHG; Great Southern Homes, Rosewood Communities)
ma.description: Merger agreement signed 22 Feb 2026 and closed 4 May 2026. All-cash, $1.18 per share, about $99.3M of equity consideration and about $221M of enterprise value. UHG became a wholly owned subsidiary, was delisted and repaid its Wells Fargo and Kennedy Lewis debt at closing. Stanley Martin's offers fell from $150M (June 2025) to $94M (Nov 2025) before the final $99.3M, and rival bids (Parties A, C, F) fell away. Vestra Advisors and Paul, Weiss advised UHG's special committee, with Maynard Nexsen for Stanley Martin.
ma.map_impact: UHG (Builder 100 #56, 1,192 closings in 2025) merges into Stanley Martin. It adds Columbia/Midlands, Upstate (Greenville-Spartanburg-Clemson), Coastal/Myrtle Beach, Augusta GA, Raleigh and the Rosewood move-up brand, plus 7,225 lots that were 96% optioned. Stanley Martin has since opened Florence SC and branded Myrtle Beach. UHG's executive officers (Jack Micenko, Keith Feldman, Michael Nieri, Tom O'Grady, Robert Penny, Jeremy Pyle, Shelton Twine) left at closing. The related-party Nieri lot pipeline was reset by the PC Property Agreements.
ma.source_title: United Homes Group 8-K filed 2026-05-04 (completion of merger with Stanley Martin Homes)
ma.note: Enterprise value and 1,192 closings from Stanley Martin's release (https://www.stanleymartin.com/blog/448/stanley-martin-homes-completes-acquisition-of-united-homes-group). Bid history and the $99,325,000 figure from the DEFM14C (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830188/000114036126014128/ny20067664x2_defm14c.htm). Myrtle Beach entry via Great Southern Homes per Stanley Martin release of Sep 2026 (https://www.stanleymartin.com/blog/455/stanley-martin-homes-expands-coastal-carolina-presence-with-entry-into-myrtle-beach-market).

ma.counterparty: Windsor Homes (Windsor Investments, LLC and affiliates), Greensboro, NC
ma.description: Announced 17 Sep 2025. Stanley Martin bought the assets and operations (land, homes, staff) and closed on 25 Sep 2025 US time. Windsor delivered 334 homes in 2024, controlled about 2,100 lots in the Triad (Greensboro, Winston-Salem, High Point, Burlington) and Wilmington, and had 270 homes under construction. Price not disclosed; Daiwa says no significant impact on results. Whelan Advisory advised Windsor (counsel Williams Parker), with Maynard Nexsen for Stanley Martin.
ma.map_impact: Adds the North Carolina Triad and Wilmington, 32 communities and roughly 25% more controlled lots in North Carolina. Tom Hall was Windsor's president. Not a ranked builder, so no Builder 100 row merges.
ma.source_title: Daiwa House press release: Stanley Martin Homes Has Acquired the Homebuilding Business of Windsor Homes (26 Sep 2025)
ma.note: Announcement details from Stanley Martin's release (https://www.stanleymartin.com/blog/429/stanley-martin-homes-to-acquire-the-assets-and-operations-of-windsor-homes-expanding-presence-in-north-carolina).

ma.counterparty: Prestige Corporate Development and Prestige Site Works (Charlotte, NC metro)
ma.description: Context, pre-2025. Stanley Martin Holdings agreed to buy a land acquisition, development and lot-sales business that controlled more than 8,000 Charlotte-area lots, plus a site-development contractor working on 15 projects (more than 2,500 lots) in North and South Carolina. Closing was expected in May 2024. Owner Brian Mahoney; Prestige president Steve Bailey.
ma.map_impact: Gives Stanley Martin an in-house lot developer and lot seller in Charlotte, so it is both a land buyer and a potential lot supplier to other builders, and a possible counterparty for land-bank structures. Daiwa lists Prestige as a wholly owned subsidiary from 2024.
ma.source_title: Stanley Martin Holdings press release: Acquires Prestige Corporate Development and Prestige Site Works (13 May 2024)
ma.note: Included for land-map context although before 2025. Closing confirmed by Daiwa's Stanley Martin page ('made Prestige Corporate Development, LLC into a wholly owned subsidiary in 2024').

industry_deals.description: Stanley Martin bought employee-owned Florida builder Holiday Builders (Melbourne FL): it agreed the deal on 2026-07-16 and the seller's adviser says it closed 2026-07-29 (other reports say it became official 2026-07-30). Price not disclosed. Holiday closed about 1,050 homes in 2025 and brings 40+ communities and about 10,600 controlled Florida lots (Palm Coast, Palm Bay, Panama City, Orlando area, North Port, Cape Coral). Holiday becomes a wholly owned subsidiary. Zelman Partners advised Holiday.
industry_deals.map_impact: Rank 62 Holiday Builders is now owned by rank 18 Stanley Martin (Daiwa House); the Holiday row merges into Stanley Martin. With UHG, Stanley Martin's 2025 pro-forma closings are about 7,560 (5,320 + 1,192 + 1,050, a sum of the figures in the cited articles), and Daiwa House's US builders total about 10,000.
industry_deals.source_title: HousingWire (sponsored, Zelman): Holiday Builders Sale Shows What Buyers Want in Homebuilder M&A (2026-07-29)

industry_deals.description: Closed 2026-05-04 (announced 2026-02-23; merger agreement dated 2026-02-22). Stanley Martin acquired Nasdaq-listed United Homes Group by merger for $1.18 per share in cash, an enterprise value of about $221 million; the stock and warrants were delisted. The executive officers listed in the closing 8-K, including chief executive Jack Micenko and executive chairman Michael Nieri, ceased to be officers at closing.
industry_deals.map_impact: United Homes Group (#56, 1,192 closings in the ranking) is now a wholly owned subsidiary of Stanley Martin (#18): the two rows share one owner, Daiwa House. United Homes' top leadership left at closing. Adds Greenville, Spartanburg, Clemson, Columbia and Myrtle Beach, South Carolina and Augusta, Georgia to Stanley Martin (per HousingWire).
industry_deals.source_title: United Homes Group 8-K filed 2026-05-04 (completion of merger with Stanley Martin Homes)

industry_deals.description: Closed 2025-09-25 US time (announced 2025-09-17). Stanley Martin bought the assets and operations of Greensboro, North Carolina builder Windsor Homes: land, homes and staff in the Triad (Greensboro, Winston-Salem, High Point) and Wilmington. Windsor delivered 334 homes in 2024 on about $124 million of revenue and had about 2,100 lots secured. Price not disclosed; Daiwa House said the effect on its results is not significant.
industry_deals.map_impact: No rank row merges (Windsor unranked). Stanley Martin (#18) adds the North Carolina Triad and Wilmington and about 2,100 lots; first of three Stanley Martin acquisitions in under a year (United Homes Group and Holiday Builders followed in 2026).
industry_deals.source_title: Daiwa House Industry press release: Stanley Martin Homes Has Acquired the Homebuilding Business of Windsor Homes (2025-09-26)

suggested_updates.text: At the Oct 2026 Zelman summit, Stanley Martin (Daiwa House) set a 10,000-closing target for 2027, said three recent acquisitions including Holiday Builders add about $1B of revenue, and is pausing single-family acquisitions to integrate them.
suggested_updates.title: Housing M&A shifts as global capital retargets residential futures

Owned versus optioned lots, total lots controlled and years of supply for Stanley Martin: not publicly disclosed. Daiwa publishes only 75,017 lots for its three US builders combined (Dec 2025). A pro-forma Stanley Martin total including UHG (7,225) and Holiday (~10,600) cannot be built.
Cash, total debt, liquidity and leverage for Stanley Martin: not publicly disclosed.

Holiday Builders and Windsor Homes purchase prices, and whether Holiday debt was assumed or repaid: not publicly disclosed.

profile.summary: Top-20 US builder: 4,947 deliveries and $3.36B of home sales revenue in 2025, 17 divisions in 13 states plus DC, and 32,444 lots owned or controlled at 2026-09-30 (16,683 owned, 15,761 controlled, about 49% controlled, per the Q3 2026 results release). financing.summary: Tri Pointe stopped being a public company on May 14, 2026, when Sumitomo Forestry (Tokyo: 1911) bought it for $47.00 a share in cash; it is now a wholly owned subsidiary of Sumitomo Forestry America and still files 10-Qs only because its two senior notes series remain outstanding. At September 30, 2026 it carried $1,103M of homebuilding debt ($300M of 5.25% notes due June 2027, $350M of 5.70% notes due June 2028, a $450M bank term loan due 2027) against an undrawn $850M revolver, $325.9M of cash and about $1.1B of liquidity. It controls 32,444 lots, 51% owned and 49% controlled; of the controlled lots about 10,000 are under option or purchase contracts ($225.9M of deposits against $1.89B of remaining purchase price) and 5,758 sit in unconsolidated land development joint ventures. Its use of land banking is small but real and recent: a first land bank financing arrangement ($19.6M of proceeds in 2025), credit-facility covenants rewritten in April 2025 to carve out lot sales under land banking arrangements, and disclosed land banking options that oblige it to finish development work even if it walks away; no land banker is named in any filing. The room for a land banker turns on the new parent: cash fell by $657M in nine months as inventory grew by $512M, about $750M of Tri Pointe debt comes due between June and September 2027, and Sumitomo Forestry's one-year JPY 835.1 billion SMBC bridge loan (sized to include an assumed refinancing of Tri Pointe's debt) falls due May 10, 2027.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed, roughly half owned and half controlled; the company does not use 'land-light' language or publish an option target. The FY2025 10-K says it buys most land under purchase agreements that are often structured as options so takedowns can be staged, uses joint ventures, options and land banking 'if necessary', and routes every acquisition through a centralized land committee. Sumitomo Forestry told analysts in February 2026 that the lot position (then 32,738) was roughly half owned and half optioned and a healthy level, and that as a public company Tri Pointe's growth investment had at times been limited by share buybacks, which ownership by Sumitomo removes.

lots.source_title: Tri Pointe Homes Q3 2026 results press release (8-K Exhibit 99.1, 2026-11-05), Lots Owned or Controlled table
lots.note: By segment (owned / controlled / total): West 8,896 / 3,594 / 12,490; Central 5,609 / 7,801 / 13,410; East 2,178 / 4,366 / 6,544. At 2025-12-31: 15,954 owned / 16,265 controlled / 32,219 total. 'Controlled' means lots under land option contracts or purchase contracts and includes the company's expected share of lots owned by unconsolidated land development joint ventures: 275 in West and 5,483 in Central at 2026-09-30 (zero and 5,356 at 2025-12-31). Excluding those 5,758 JV lots, 10,003 lots are under option or purchase contracts (our subtraction). pct_optioned is our calculation (15,761 / 32,444). years_supply is our calculation, not a company figure: 32,444 lots over 4,197 trailing-twelve-month deliveries (FY2025 4,947 less nine months 2025 3,583 plus nine months 2026 2,833). Sumitomo Forestry's February 2026 briefing described the position as about six and a half years of supply on FY2024 volumes.

land_banking.counterparty: Undisclosed land banker (land bank financing arrangement, 2025)
land_banking.description: Tri Pointe sold land under a land bank financing arrangement and kept an option to buy it back, so the sale is booked as a financing: the land stays on the balance sheet as consolidated inventory not owned. The cash flow statement shows $19.6M of proceeds from the arrangement in 2025 and none in the first nine months of 2026.
land_banking.source_title: Tri Pointe Homes Form 10-K for fiscal year 2025 (filed 2026-02-26), Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows
land_banking.note: First appeared in Q3 2025: no such line in the Q1 2025 cash flow and inventory not owned was all deposits at 2025-06-30; $12.8M of proceeds by 2025-09-30 and $19.6M for the full year. Consolidated inventory not owned was $19.6M at 2025-12-31 and $14.4M at 2026-09-30 (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1561680/000156168026000047/R10.htm). Counterparty, lot count, location and pricing are not disclosed. No comparable line in 2023 or 2024.

land_banking.counterparty: Undisclosed land bankers (option-based land banking arrangements)
land_banking.description: The variable interest entity note says Tri Pointe has entered into land banking arrangements under which it must complete the development work even if it terminates its option to buy the land or lots. These sit inside its option agreements with unconsolidated VIEs; the land banking share is not broken out.
land_banking.source_title: Tri Pointe Homes Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (filed 2026-11-05), Note 6 Variable Interest Entities
land_banking.note: Option agreements with unconsolidated VIEs (land bankers and other sellers together): $215.4M of deposits and $1,817.3M of remaining purchase price at 2026-09-30 ($201.6M and $1,960.5M at 2025-12-31). The same sentence appears in the FY2025 10-K. The April 30, 2025 credit agreement modification changed financial covenants to exclude the impact of lot sales under land banking arrangements (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1561680/000156168025000062/tph-20250430.htm), and the debt note describes interest incurred as covering 'all debt and land banking'. No counterparty is named.

land_banking.counterparty: Land sellers and developers under option and purchase contracts (not named)
land_banking.description: All land and lot option and purchase agreements together: $225.9M of non-refundable deposits securing $1,886.6M of remaining purchase price at September 30, 2026, covering about 10,000 controlled lots outside joint ventures.
land_banking.source_title: Tri Pointe Homes Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (filed 2026-11-05), Note 6 Variable Interest Entities
land_banking.note: Split: unconsolidated VIEs $215.4M deposits / $1,817.3M remaining price; other option agreements $10.5M / $69.3M. At 2025-12-31: $209.6M deposits / $2,069.4M remaining price. Capitalized pre-acquisition costs $12.5M. lots (10,003) is our subtraction: 15,761 controlled lots less 5,758 JV lots, from the Q3 2026 release (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1561680/000156168026000044/tphex991q32026.htm). Option abandonment and pre-acquisition charges were $13.5M in the first nine months of 2026, including a $9.0M Q2 charge for optioned lots in one West community that the company chose not to buy. Some sellers are master developers with repurchase rights (FY2025 10-K).

land_banking.counterparty: Unconsolidated land development joint ventures (partners not named)
land_banking.description: Tri Pointe counts its expected share of lots owned by unconsolidated land development joint ventures as controlled lots: 5,758 at September 30, 2026 (275 West, 5,483 Central, the segment covering Texas, Colorado and Utah). That is 37% of all controlled lots, held off balance sheet with partner capital and JV-level debt.
land_banking.source_title: Tri Pointe Homes Q3 2026 results press release (8-K Exhibit 99.1, 2026-11-05), footnote to Lots Owned or Controlled table
land_banking.note: 5,356 lots (all Central) at 2025-12-31. Partner names, which projects, and the takedown terms are not disclosed. See joint_ventures for the JV balance sheet.

debt.instrument: PARENT LEVEL (Sumitomo Forestry Co., Ltd., not a Tri Pointe obligation): acquisition bridge loan, up to JPY 835.1 billion
debt.source_title: Sumitomo Forestry: Notice Regarding the Conclusion of a Loan Agreement with Financial Covenants (2026-05-07)
debt.note: Yen loan signed May 7, 2026, drawn about May 11, bullet repayment planned May 10, 2027. JPY 835.1 billion is the maximum and, by Sumitomo's own footnote, includes funds for the assumed refinancing of Tri Pointe's existing debt on top of the roughly JPY 630 billion share price. Covenants: consolidated and parent net assets at least 75% of the prior year, and an R&I issuer rating of BBB- or higher. Sumitomo says it will refinance into long-term funding within about a year; JPY 350 billion of hybrid bonds and a subordinated loan were raised in September 2026 toward repayment (see capital_events). The balance still outstanding today is not disclosed in the notices read.

ma.counterparty: Sumitomo Forestry Co., Ltd. (through Sumitomo Forestry America, Inc.)
ma.description: All-cash acquisition of 100% of Tri Pointe at $47.00 per share, announced February 13, 2026 and closed May 14, 2026 by reverse triangular merger with Teton NewCo, Inc. About $4.5B transaction value; Sumitomo put the price for the shares at about $4,003M at closing.
ma.map_impact: Ownership changes from Public to subsidiary of a foreign company; parent is Sumitomo Forestry (Tokyo: 1911) via Sumitomo Forestry America. The spine row still shows Public. Tri Pointe keeps its brand, its Irvine home office, its 17 divisions and its management (CEO Doug Bauer and President and COO Tom Mitchell per the closing release; Glenn Keeler signed the November 5, 2026 8-K as CFO); the five outside directors named in the closing 8-K resigned. It becomes a second US platform beside Sumitomo's five existing builders (MainVue Homes, Bloomfield Homes, Brightland Homes, DRB Group, Edge Homes); Sumitomo says it has no plan to merge the platforms now. The group claims a pro forma rank equal to fifth in the US, about 15,000 homes a year across 18 states and roughly 114,000 lots. For financing: capital decisions now run through a Japanese parent that funds in yen, buybacks have stopped, and public lot and debt disclosure will end once the 2027 and 2028 notes are repaid.
ma.source_title: Tri Pointe Homes 8-K (completion of merger), filed 2026-05-14
ma.note: after_ranking is true because the deal closed on May 14, 2026 and the closing release already cites the 2026 Builder 100; it was announced on February 13, before the ranking. The Builder 100 row (4,947 closings in 2025) is Tri Pointe standalone. Tri Pointe's president received a $10.9M retention bonus at closing; the CEO, CFO and general counsel also have retention agreements dated February 13, 2026. Advisors: Moelis and Paul Hastings for Tri Pointe; Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley / Morgan Stanley and Morrison & Foerster for Sumitomo. Sumitomo said talks with Tri Pointe's founders ran for about two years. Per the merger proxy (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1561680/000119312526110678/d114079ddefm14a.htm), the CEOs first met on May 16, 2024; Sumitomo bid $41.00 on December 1, 2025 (rejected), $45.00 on December 11 and $47.00 on January 16, 2026; the board did not solicit other bidders.

industry_deals.description: Sumitomo Forestry completed its all-cash purchase of NYSE-listed Tri Pointe Homes on 2026-05-14 (merger agreement dated 2026-02-13); Tri Pointe survived as an indirect wholly owned subsidiary of Sumitomo Forestry and deregistered its shares (SEC filing). Per trade press the price was $47.00 per share, about $4.5B; Tri Pointe keeps its brand, Irvine home office and management under CEO Doug Bauer; it had 160+ active communities, and with Sumitomo's five existing US builders the group expects about 15,000 US homes a year across 18 states against a 23,000-a-year 2030 goal. In November 2026 Sumitomo cut its 2026 US closings forecast to 12,705 (from 14,160) and called Tri Pointe synergies with its other US builders its top priority.
industry_deals.map_impact: Rank 19 Tri Pointe Homes is no longer a listed company; it becomes a sister of rank 15 DRB Group (builder_id drb-group) (Sumitomo Forestry's other top-100 builder) and Sumitomo's other US builders. The Tri Pointe row stays as a separate brand but its parent changes to Sumitomo Forestry; combined Sumitomo US volume is roughly top-five scale. Leadership stayed. Watch for consolidation between Tri Pointe and the other Sumitomo builders in 2027.

Credit ratings (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) for Tri Pointe: not stated in the filings opened, and rating-agency releases could not be searched for. Left blank rather than filled from memory. Parent-level: Sumitomo Forestry's bridge loan requires an R&I issuer rating of BBB- or higher.

The bridge loan was sized for an 'assumed refinancing' of Tri Pointe debt, but all of it was still outstanding at September 30, 2026 and no intercompany loan or parent guarantee appears in the Q3 2026 10-Q notes.
Joint-venture partner names (17 unconsolidated entities, including the land development JVs behind 5,758 controlled lots) and the financial services JV partner: not publicly disclosed.

M&A by Tri Pointe as acquirer in 2025 or 2026: none appears in the FY2025 10-K cash flow statement, the 2025 to 2026 8-K list or the Q3 2026 10-Q. Trade press was not searched for small unannounced deals.

financing.summary: LGI Homes is one of the most land-heavy public builders: at September 30, 2026 it owned 50,270 of its 58,400 lots (86%) and controlled only 8,130 (14%) through ordinary purchase and option contracts, and its CEO describes the position as predominantly self-developed and on balance sheet. It funds land with a roughly $1.17 billion bank revolver agented by Wells Fargo (borrowing base tied to land, lots and homes; $411.2 million drawn at quarter-end) plus $1.1 billion of senior notes due 2028, 2029 and 2032, and a $50 million non-recourse loan against its rental homes. Its only disclosed land-banking program, with one unnamed third-party land banker, ran from 2022 and was fully repurchased by June 30, 2026, so LGI currently has no land banker. Net debt to capital is 40.6%, high for the group, the lot supply is about 12 years at the 2026 closing pace, two thirds of owned lots are still raw or under development, and the credit agreement blocks buybacks and dividends through December 31, 2026: that combination (heavy owned land, elevated leverage, nothing due in 2026 or 2027 but $400 million of 8.75% notes due December 2028, and management saying it now sees more finished-lot takedown opportunities) is the opening for a land banker.
financing.land_strategy: Owns most. Company framing: a 'flexible land acquisition strategy' of buying or optioning finished lots or buying raw land for development, with land banking used 'on a limited and strategic basis' (FY2025 10-K); the CEO calls the position 'predominantly self-developed, on-balance-sheet' (Q3 2026 release). No stated owned/optioned target or years-of-supply target. Raw land takes two to four years to become an active community. Direction of travel: owned lots have fallen six straight quarters from a peak of 61,893 (Q2 2022) while controlled lots rose 18.1% in Q3 2026 as management pursued finished-lot takedowns from developers and smaller projects.

lots.source_title: LGI Homes Q3 2026 results press release (8-K Exhibit 99.1), filed 2026-11-03
lots.note: Owned 50,270 = 34,119 raw/under development + 16,151 finished (the finished count includes 2,147 completed homes and information centers and 1,626 homes in progress; about 12,378 vacant finished lots per the earnings call). 'Optioned' is the company's 'controlled' figure. years_supply is computed, not company-stated: 58,400 lots divided by the 4,700 midpoint of 2026 closings guidance (4,600 to 4,800). The Q3 2026 10-Q Note 10 separately shows 8,622 lots under land option and purchase contracts ($390.6M aggregate purchase price, $17.9M deposits); the 492-lot difference from 8,130 is not reconciled in the filing. Trend: 70,899 lots at 12/31/2024, 60,842 at 12/31/2025 (51,890 owned / 8,952 controlled), 59,028 at 3/31/2026, 57,406 at 6/30/2026. Segment split at 12/31/2025 (owned/controlled): Central 19,108/517; Southeast 13,372/2,629; Northwest 5,877/1,250; West 8,367/3,323; Florida 5,166/1,233 (FY2025 10-K). The 9/30/2026 segment split was not retrievable.

land_banking.counterparty: Undisclosed third-party land banker (LGI filings do not name it)
land_banking.description: CONCLUDED. LGI sold land to a single third-party land banker under 'several' financing arrangements and bought it back as finished lots in staged takedowns, paying a non-refundable commitment fee for the repurchase option; it was not legally obliged to take the remaining lots but faced penalties if it did not. LGI accounted for it as a financing (real estate not owned with a matching liability). The balance ran down from $141.8M (12/31/2022) to $118.9M (9/30/2023), $37.1M (12/31/2024), $13.6M (9/30/2025), $8.0M (12/31/2025) and zero: all lots were repurchased by June 30, 2026.
land_banking.source_title: LGI Homes Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (Notes 2, 3 and 10)
land_banking.note: amount_usd_m left null because the program is fully repaid; the largest balance found in the filings opened was $141.8M at 12/31/2022. Payments to the land banker were $67.9M in 2024 and $29.9M in 2025 (FY2025 10-K MD&A). Lot count, fee/yield and the date and size of each sale were not disclosed in the filings read. Earlier balances from the Q3 2023, Q1 2025 and Q3 2025 10-Qs listed in sources_consulted.

land_banking.counterparty: Various land sellers and lot developers (not named)
land_banking.description: Ordinary land purchase and option contracts, not land banking: 8,622 lots under contract at September 30, 2026 for an aggregate purchase price of $390.6M, secured by $17.9M of deposits and option payments (about $11.0M of that on finished-lot contracts and refundable in certain circumstances). Exposure is generally limited to forfeiting the non-refundable deposits. Up from 7,388 lots / $257.0M at June 30, 2026 as management added finished-lot takedowns.
land_banking.source_title: LGI Homes Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (Note 10, Commitments and Contingencies)
land_banking.note: At 12/31/2025: 8,952 lots, $285.7M purchase price, $19.2M deposits. The earnings release counts 8,130 controlled lots at the same date; the difference is not explained.

Commitments after the amendment: $1,165.98M plus a $175.0M incremental facility. Staggered maturity: $855.0M (73.3%) on October 9, 2030; 18.4% (about $215M) on April 28, 2029; 8.3% (about $96M) on April 28, 2028. Before the amendment: $1.1825B, $972.5M due April 2029 and 17.8% due April 2028. Lenders (Schedule I): Wells Fargo $135M; Fifth Third, Bank of America, Citizens $130M each; BMO $125.4M; U.S. Bank $110M; Huntington $80M; Flagstar $75M; Regions $72.3M; First National Bank of Pennsylvania $48.2M (non-extending); Texas Capital $48.2M; Third Coast $45M; Woodforest $20M; Hancock Whitney $9.6M; Chang Hwa $7.2M. Guaranteed by subsidiaries with gross assets of at least $0.5M, except the subsidiaries that only own and operate single-family rental homes; the borrowing base is the land, lots and homes held by LGI and those guarantors. LGI may ask for a one-year extension before each anniversary. Borrowing-base advance rates include 50% land held for development, 65% lots under development, 70% finished lots. Covenants: minimum tangible net worth, maximum leverage, minimum liquidity, minimum EBITDA to interest; buybacks and dividends restricted through December 31, 2026. financing.summary: Beazer Homes is no longer a stand-alone borrower: Dream Finders Homes bought it for $33.50 a share in cash (about $878.4M of equity) on 2026-10-20, and Beazer's land and debt now sit inside Dream Finders' land-light, option-heavy model. Before the deal Beazer owned about 40% of its active lots and funded itself with a JPMorgan-led $525M unsecured revolver, $1.0B of senior notes and $100.8M face of junior subordinated notes (net debt to net capital 52.8% at 2026-06-30, up from 39.5% a year earlier). At closing Millrose Properties (managed by Kennedy Lewis) bought about 7,000 Beazer homesites, more than half finished, for about $580M and optioned them back to Dream Finders; that money retired Beazer's 2029 notes and revolver. What is left of Beazer's own capital structure is $650M of 2031 and 2032 notes, almost all being swapped into Dream Finders paper (settlement expected 2026-11-23), and the junior subordinated notes. For a competing land banker, Beazer's remaining owned land and any future land-bank work are now Dream Finders decisions, and Millrose is already in both the land and the capital structure.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed, moving toward more options. Beazer bought lots through option agreements 'with land developers and land bankers' and expected to exercise substantially all of them; it raised the optioned share of active lots from 57.8% (FY2024) to 62.1% (FY2025), then 60.0% at 2026-06-30. No numeric optioned-lot target was stated; its stated FY2027 goals were more than 200 active communities, net debt to net capital in the low 30% range, and book value per share in the mid-$50s. It also sold non-strategic land (more than $100M expected in FY2026, per the CEO) and did a model-home sale-leaseback. Since 2026-10-20 the land is run under Dream Finders' 'asset-light' finished-lot and land-bank option model.

lots.source_title: Beazer Homes fiscal Q3 2026 earnings release (8-K Ex. 99.1)
lots.note: Reported: 24,489 total controlled lots and 23,083 active lots, 60.0% of active lots under option (last reported quarter before the merger; Beazer stopped filing after 2026-10-20). Owned and optioned counts are computed, not reported: optioned = 60.0% x 23,083 = about 13,850; owned = 24,489 - 13,850 = about 10,639 (includes about 1,406 lots held for future development or for sale). pct_optioned is the share of active lots. At 2025-09-30 the 10-K showed 25,660 controlled, 24,758 active, 15,373 optioned (62.1%) and 10,287 owned. Years of supply not stated. At closing about 7,000 of the owned homesites moved to Millrose under options to Dream Finders, so the owned share is now far lower.

ma.counterparty: Dream Finders Homes, Inc.
ma.description: Dream Finders acquired Beazer in an all-cash merger at $33.50 a share (about $878.4M of equity), and Beazer became a wholly owned subsidiary and delisted. Dream Finders approached privately on 2026-01-16, offered $28.50 (Feb) and $29.00 (Mar), went public on 2026-05-11 with a $25.75 offer the board rejected, raised to $29.25 (June 22) and $32.00 (June 30, public 2026-07-08), and signed at $33.50 on 2026-08-06 (announced 2026-08-07) after rival bidders withdrew. Funded with Series B preferred, Millrose land banking, revolver borrowings and cash. Beazer's advisors were J.P. Morgan and Moelis.
ma.map_impact: Fold Beazer under Dream Finders: it is no longer a separate public builder or borrower. All nine Beazer directors (including Allan Merrill) resigned and were replaced by Dream Finders' directors (Patrick Zalupski, Rick Beckwitt and others); Beazer's officers stayed in their roles at closing (CFO David I. Goldberg signed the closing 8-K), but the combined land and division reporting lines are not published. The JPMorgan revolver and 2029 notes are gone; the 2031 and 2032 notes are becoming Dream Finders notes; about 7,000 Beazer homesites are now Millrose land under option to Dream Finders. Beazer's markets (AZ, CA, NV, TX, IN, MD/DE, TN, VA, FL, GA, NC, SC) are now Dream Finders markets, so land calls go to the Dream Finders team.
ma.source_title: Beazer Homes USA Form 8-K (merger closing, 2026-10-20)
ma.note: Offer history from the DEFM14A background section. Dream Finders closing 8-K gives the $878.4M equity consideration.

ma.counterparty: Party B (unnamed strategic bidder)
ma.description: Unnamed strategic bidder contacted 2026-05-11; offered $32.00 cash (June 19) and $33.50 cash (July 9), holding about 3% of Beazer stock; withdrew on 2026-08-02 citing higher financing costs and operational limits in its proposed land bank financing. Party C (strategic, part-stock $32.00 offer on July 2) withdrew 2026-07-29 citing share price, execution risk and land-banking financing; Party A (a real estate developer) proposed contributing its US homebuilding operations for 27% to 40% of the combined company and was not pursued.
ma.map_impact: No change to the map; shows that at least two other builders bidding for Beazer planned to fund it with land-bank capital and walked away over its cost and terms.
ma.source_title: Beazer Homes USA DEFM14A merger proxy statement
ma.note: Bidder identities not disclosed in the proxy.

industry_deals.description: Dream Finders completed its all-cash purchase of Beazer on 2026-10-20 at $33.50 per share, about $2.2B enterprise value; Beazer was delisted from the NYSE. Dream Finders expects $100M+ of annual run-rate cost synergies, will move Beazer communities onto Dream Finders floor plans and aims to bring leverage back to current levels within 18-24 months. The combined company builds in 26 of the top 50 MSAs. Millrose provided about $1.07B of land-bank and preferred-equity financing (see the Millrose profile).
industry_deals.map_impact: Rank 21 Beazer Homes merges into rank 14 Dream Finders Homes; the Beazer row disappears and the combined company calls itself the 6th largest US builder (by 2025 revenue; HousingWire counts 13,035 combined 2025 closings). Adds California, Nevada, Indiana and Delaware and more Maryland/DC to Dream Finders. Patrick Zalupski stays CEO and co-chairman; Rick Beckwitt (ex-Lennar and D.R. Horton) joined the Dream Finders board as co-chairman in July 2026 during the bid. The closing release names no continuing role for Beazer CEO Allan Merrill or other Beazer executives.

Regional president for Southeast (FL, GA, NC, SC): not publicly disclosed

Troy Radelat and Steven Cervino appear as 'Area President' only on ZoomInfo/The Org snippets (not sources), and Jay Thrower (Area President, Charleston and Myrtle Beach, Feb 2018 release) has no 2025-2026 confirmation; none carried.

Post-merger regional structure: Dream Finders' Q3 2026 10-Q (period to 2026-09-30) keeps its Southeast / Mid-Atlantic / Midwest segments and does not assign the Beazer divisions; HousingWire's integration pieces (2026-08-03, 2026-08-11) name no Beazer regional or land leaders.

Corporate land head: Senior Vice President of Land Acquisition (referenced in job postings) still unnamed after a second targeted pass; a search for Erica Champion (The Org 'Chief Investment Officer') found no confirming source.

No leader is publicly named for these markets as of 2025-2026: Southern California (Riverside-San Bernardino), San Diego, Las Vegas, Dallas/Fort Worth, Houston, San Antonio, Indianapolis, Maryland/Baltimore, Northern Virginia/DC, Orlando, Charleston and Myrtle Beach. Beazer.com market pages, event pages and blog posts name no staff. The 2025-2026 company releases quote only the CEO and CMO, apart from the Phoenix release and the March 2026 Fisher House caption.

Area presidents / regional market leaders: Beazer's FY2025 10-K says these roles lead the divisions and report to the CEO, but no filing, company page or release opened in this run names any of them. Leads seen only on third-party directories (ZoomInfo / Yahoo Finance via search snippets; not sources, so not carried as rows): Troy Radelat and Steven Cervino (Area President), Bruce Craig (Area President), and Gary Szebalskie, Jason Oates, Shane Anthony, David Little and Christopher Gillen (Division President). None of these has a market or date attached.

Stale names not carried: Jay Thrower, named Area President for Charleston and Myrtle Beach in February 2018 (search result only, no 2025-2026 confirmation); Tim Little, named Phoenix Division President in 2014; Ed Gold, named Maryland Division President in 2012 and quoted in 2013; Ryan Johnson, Phoenix division president in 2024, succeeded by Joe Vannelli by August 2025; Geoff Hart, Nashville division president in October 2023.

Division and regional land leaders (VP / Director of Land Acquisition, Land Development, Entitlement): none are named in any public source found. Beazer's buy-or-sell-land page is a single form that names no contact. A search result showed a job posting for a 'Division Vice President of Land Acquisition' in Myrtle Beach (careerbuilder), which confirms that division-level land VP roles exist, but no name was given. The legacy iCIMS job board now redirects to careers.beazer.com / careers.dreamfindershomes.com.

Owned versus optioned lot counts at 2026-06-30: only the 60.0% optioned share of active lots was reported; counts are computed. No lot data after 2026-06-30 (Beazer stopped reporting; Dream Finders has not published Beazer's post-Millrose lot split).
Years of lot supply: not stated by Beazer.
Option fee rate and terms on the Millrose homesites: not publicly disclosed beyond about 2.5-year weighted-average life.

Consent fee paid to 2031/2032 noteholders: not stated in Beazer's 8-K.
Post-merger credit ratings on Beazer or its notes: not checked in a public source.
Joint ventures: none disclosed in the FY2025 10-K or FY2026 10-Qs read.
Model-home sale-leaseback counterparty and proceeds: not publicly disclosed.
Beazer acquisitions or divestitures in 2025-2026 other than the Dream Finders merger: none found in the 8-K list (no Item 2.01 filings before the merger closing).
Identities of rival bidders (Parties A to D) and their land-bank financiers: not publicly disclosed.

land_banker_links.what: At the Dream Finders closing, certain pre-acquisition Beazer land assets were sold to Millrose and Dream Finders got options to buy the homesites over time on terms like its other land-bank options. Millrose says it fun…

Commitment letter signed with the merger agreement on 2026-08-06: an $800M land bank facility to fund part of the Beazer purchase price, conditioned on the merger, the preferred investment and a notes or equity offering…

profile.org_note: Three tiers: CEO and President Todd Chachere, then regional Presidents (Perry's internal title is City President: Matthew Gerdes for Houston, Billy Shirley for Dallas-Fort Worth, Chris Little for Central Texas and Florida), then 19 Division Presidents (e.g. Garrison Taska for most of Florida, Brad Shee for Jacksonville). Land deals run through the land affiliates PH Land Holdings, LLC and PH Land Holdings HOU, LLC, whose officers are Chachere, CFO and Treasurer Eric Bakk, CLAO Michael Brisch, SVP Land Nick McIntyre and the Texas City Presidents Gerdes, Shirley and Little; those are the land decision-makers.
profile.summary: Private, woman-owned Houston builder founded in 1967, now in nine markets: Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin and San Antonio in Texas, and Jacksonville, Orlando, Tampa, Southeast and Southwest Florida. The company reports more than 73,000 homeowners served and more than 140 communities, and bought Jacksonville's MasterCraft Builder Group in December 2024. State records show it holds land through its own affiliates (PH Land Holdings) with a dedicated SVP Land, which suggests it owns and develops some of its lots rather than only buying finished lots in master plans; the Florida build-out is the newest likely call for lot capital.

financing.summary: Perry Homes is a family-owned private builder (Owner and Executive Chair Kathy Perry Britton) with no public debt, no SEC filings and no credit rating, so its bank lines, lenders, leverage and lot position are not public. Its land model is to buy finished lots from master-plan developers through builder programs: in its own words it 'relies on strong developer partnerships', and every Florida entry since 2024 has been announced alongside a named developer (Eisenhower, GreenPointe, Forestar, Metro Development, Tavistock, Wheelock/Gentry, Brookfield Kolter, Raydient). The exceptions are Juniper Springs in Lockhart, TX, where Perry is itself the developer of about 1,400 homesites, and new acreage-lot product in Central Texas and Dallas-Fort Worth. No land banker or lot-option financier is publicly linked to Perry. The opening for a land banker is the Florida build-out (five markets and about 15 communities in under three years, plus the December 2024 MasterCraft purchase in Jacksonville) and Perry's first self-developed community, both of which need more land capital than the Texas finished-lot business has historically required.
financing.land_strategy: Finished-lot buyer in third-party master-planned communities, plus selective self-development. Company framing: 'We rely on strong developer partnerships' (Chris Little, President of Central Texas and Florida, July 2026) and growth 'driven by ... partnering with best-in-class developers' (April 2026 release). Perry acts as developer at Juniper Springs, Lockhart (about 1,400 homes). No owned-versus-optioned target or land-light goal has been stated publicly.

land_banking.description: Perry Homes is itself the developer and the only builder at Juniper Springs in Lockhart (Austin area), planned for about 1,400 homes on 45', 50' and 60' lots with a third of the land kept as open space and an on-site elementary school. The community site calls it Perry's move into development and a 'legacy project'. Sales inquiries opened June 2025; grand opening May 2026.

land_banking.note: This is owned and developed land, the capital-heavy exception to Perry's finished-lot model, and the clearest opening for land-bank or development capital. How Perry funds the development (bank debt, equity, district reimbursements) is not disclosed. Home count is from Perry's July 2025 release (company-news/perry-homes-continues-tradition-of-excellence-with-new-juniper-springs-community-in-lockhart).

profile.org_note: Not a for-sale builder: a private, vertically integrated rental-housing developer with four operating companies (development, construction, property management, investment management) under founder-CEO Chris Finlay and a small partner group. Land is sourced centrally by Head of Land Acquisitions Reece Kimsey (5-person team) and locally by market Development Partners, who each lead sourcing, capitalization, entitlement and construction and roll up to a Regional Development Partner. Capital sits with the development capital markets and private capital heads (TJ Sedeski, Brooks Honeycutt) and partners Corey Gibson and Rachel Noone. The finance and capital bench turned over in 2026: the CIO, a CFO, the head of capital markets and the Southeast regional head have all dropped off the company site (see notes). TX, AZ and CO are new 2026 markets with staff but no announced projects yet. Main phone is the issuer phone on the firm's SEC Form D filings (1921 Gallows Road, Suite 700, Vienna, VA 22182); the site publishes only info@livemiddleburg.com.
profile.summary: NOT A CONVENTIONAL HOMEBUILDER and a weak fit for lot-option land banking. Middleburg is a private developer, builder and operator of rental housing (Mosby apartments, Hamlet single-family build-to-rent, Vesta workforce housing); its 4,150 Builder 100 'closings' are 2025 rental unit starts (NMHC No. 11 developer, No. 13 builder), not home sales. It has 52 projects and 18,000+ units under control, about 5,600 under construction, and plans 18 to 20 starts in 2026 across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic plus a new Western platform (Dallas, Phoenix, Denver). It ties up sites under contract, entitles them with its own GP fund money and closes land with construction financing, so there is no finished-lot takedown stream; the only plausible angle for a land banker is pre-development land carry on BTR or apartment sites.

financing.summary: NOT A FOR-SALE HOMEBUILDER: Middleburg develops, builds and operates rental housing (apartments and Hamlet single-family build-to-rent), so it does not buy finished lots on a takedown schedule and is at best an edge-case land-banking customer. It funds each project separately: institutional joint-venture equity (Harbor Group International is the one LP named in 2026), its own GP co-invest from a discretionary fund series (GP Fund III closed at $125M in February 2026), bank construction loans (Truist and US Bank named) and agency take-out debt (Freddie Mac via Newmark). Sites are held under contract while GP fund money carries them through zoning and entitlement, and land usually closes together with the construction loan, which removes most of the need for a third-party land banker. The room for one is narrow: pre-development land carry or horizontal development on BTR sites if its 52-project, 18,000-unit pipeline outruns GP fund capital, especially in the new Western markets. The firm is also a capital provider (preferred equity and mezzanine funds for other sponsors), and its finance bench turned over in 2026, so relationships there are in flux. Corporate debt, cash and leverage are not public.
financing.land_strategy: Capital-light site control rather than land ownership: the land team sources off-market sites directly (750+ scored and 30+ contracted a year across eight states and 30+ metros), holds them under contract through entitlement, and closes the land when construction financing is in place. No stated owned/optioned target because it does not operate a lot pipeline. Company figures: 52 projects and 18,000+ units under control and in development, about 20 projects and 5,600 units under construction, 18 to 20 starts planned for 2026.

land_banking.description: The firm's own discretionary GP fund plays the role a land banker would: it funds the sponsor's equity and the pursuit phase. A development partner told the Phoenix Business Journal in June 2026 that a general partner fund lets him put sites under contract and carry them through zoning and entitlement. No third-party land banker or lot-option partner has been named publicly.
land_banking.source_title: Middleburg press release: GP Fund III final close at $125 million
land_banking.note: Fund size from the company release; the pursuit and entitlement use is from the Phoenix Business Journal article reposted at https://www.middleburg.com/news/virginia-real-estate-firm-taps-phoenix-partner-for-arizona-expansion (Reported).

profile.org_note: Mattamy publishes no regional layer, but its live Charlotte and Raleigh 'Division President' job postings (seen 2026-11-19) say the role 'Reports to: Regional President', so at least the Carolinas divisions sit under an unnamed regional president; the four regions here are state groupings for this map, not a company-published list. About ten division presidents (Phoenix, Tucson, Tampa, Southwest Florida, Orlando, Jacksonville, Southeast Florida, Charlotte, Raleigh, Dallas) run the markets under US CEO Chris Lindhorst (since 2026-09-01); Wellen Park runs separately as a master-developer business. Each division has a VP of Land under the division president, and division land teams send land reports to the corporate office and present deals to a 'senior investment committee' (job postings); no corporate land head is named. Finance and capital decisions sit at the Toronto parent (CFO Bill Tofflemire; Vice Chair Larry Nicholson oversees US and Canadian homebuilding).
profile.summary: Mattamy Homes US is the US arm of Toronto-based, Gilgan family-owned Mattamy, the largest family-owned homebuilder in North America (about 8,300 closings and US$5.9B revenue for the group, LTM to Aug 2026). It runs about 11 US markets weighted to Florida, plus the Carolinas, Arizona and Dallas. It is a land developer as well as a builder: it owns the 10,000-acre Wellen Park master plan and buys large raw-land tracts. 2026 releases show steady land buying in Arizona and Tampa, and a new US CEO (ex-D.R. Horton regional president Chris Lindhorst) since September 2026.

financing.summary: Mattamy Homes U.S. does not borrow on its own. It is funded centrally by its Canadian parent, Mattamy Group Corporation (owned through Mattamy Asset Management, the Gilgan family holding company), which issues Rule 144A/Reg S senior unsecured notes in US$ and C$ and runs one cross-border bank revolver that funds both countries. In December 2025 the group sold US$475M of 6.00% notes due 2033 and C$350M of new notes. It used the proceeds to retire its US$500M 5.25% notes due 2027 and C$250M 4.625% notes due 2028 and to pay down the revolver. That leaves no bond maturity before the US$ 4.625% notes due March 2030. The bank line is a three-year, $2.1B sustainability-linked revolver set up in fall 2024, so its renewal (about fall 2027) is the next big refinancing date. Mattamy is a land developer as much as a builder: it is master developer and majority landowner at Wellen Park (Venice, FL) and develops Tradition (Port St. Lucie, FL). Its 2025-2026 US land releases describe outright closings, either raw land or finished lots bought from master developers, and none mentions a land banker or option partner. That makes Mattamy an under-penetrated prospect for land banking, not an existing land-bank user. Owned-versus-optioned lot data is not public: financial statements go only to certified noteholders through Intralinks.
financing.land_strategy: Owns most / developer model, inferred from the company's own releases. Mattamy calls itself master developer and majority landowner at Wellen Park (22,500 homes at build-out) and develops Tradition (Port St. Lucie). Its 2025-2026 US land announcements are outright purchases. Examples: 76 acres in Fort Mill, SC for $13M (193 homes); 65 and 29 acres near Charlotte (187 + 61 homes); 70 finished lots in Avondale, AZ for $6.37M; 145 lots at Verona (Pasco County, FL), a master plan led by Eisenhower Property Group; 154 lots at Twin Peaks Crossings (Marana, AZ); and 59 and 71 finished lots in Glendale and Tucson, AZ (both closed 2026-10-29). Mattamy publishes no optioned-lot target and has never disclosed a land-light goal.

profile.org_note: Partner-run private builder: three managing partners (Saun Sullivan, CEO; Jeff Purpera Jr., CFO; Lee Foster, COO) make the land and finance decisions, and local land records show Purpera personally signing lot purchases. The site lists seven operating areas with their own offices (Louisiana, North Alabama, South Alabama, Florida, Mississippi, Tennessee, Texas) under affiliated entities DSLD Homes, LLC; DSLD Homes (Gulf Coast), LLC; DSLD Homes (Florida), LLC; DSLD Homes (Southwest), LLC; and DSLD Homes (Southeast), LLC, but names no area or division leader. Purpera and Foster are also the listed directors of Pavo Capital Inc., a Baton Rouge lot-holding company active in 2025.

profile.summary: Largest private homebuilder in the Gulf South: 120+ active communities across Louisiana, southern Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee, Texas and Northwest Florida, and homes built for 41,000+ families, selling entry-level 'affordable quality' homes. Baton Rouge Business Report put it in the local $1 billion revenue club in Nov 2025, with 550+ staff, 20-plus offices and Louisiana down to about 65% of closings from 95%. It mostly buys finished lots in phases from local developers (repeated recorded takedowns in 2024 to 2026), and the partners run a related lot-holding company, so a land banker's counterparty is the three-partner group, above all the CFO.

financing.summary: DSLD Homes is a private builder run by its managing partners (CEO Saun Sullivan, CFO Jeff Purpera, Lee Foster) that publishes no financial statements, so its lenders, debt and lot counts are not public. What is on the record is how it gets land: it buys finished lots a filing at a time (roughly 26 to 110 lots per deed, about $60,000 a lot in the Baton Rouge region) from local third-party developers and from development entities its own partners sign for, so developers and partner affiliates carry the land that a land banker would otherwise carry. Its CFO said in November 2025 that 'bankers and bondholders' ask how big it plans to get, which indicates bank debt and some form of bonds, with no terms disclosed. No institutional land banker or lot-option financier is named anywhere, and no link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. Room for a land banker looks real but relationship-driven: the company crossed $1B of revenue, is spreading into Tennessee and Houston where it lacks its home-market developer network, and its principals already run their own lot-holding vehicle (Pavo Capital).
financing.land_strategy: Finished-lot buyer, in effect land-light without calling itself that. It takes lots down by subdivision filing from local developers on a steady 'even flow' build schedule, and sources part of its supply from land entities tied to its own partners (Livingston Parc LLC, Noco LLC). In 2018 the partners said they bought about 250 lots a month; no current figure or stated owned-versus-optioned target is published.

financing.summary: Green Brick is a land-heavy, self-developing builder: at 2026-09-30 it owned 79.5% of 51,435 lots, develops most of them itself in infill and infill-adjacent DFW, Atlanta, Austin and Houston submarkets, and says on every call that it does not use land banking (Co-CEO Jim Brickman calls it high-interest money paid at 8-12% that shifts control of takedown timing to the land banker). It funds land from operating cash flow, a $330M unsecured revolver (Flagstar agent; $105M drawn at Q3 2026), about $188M of low-coupon (3.25-3.35%) privately placed senior notes amortising through 2029, and $50M of 5.75% perpetual preferred; homebuilding debt-to-capital is 13.1% (net 9.6%). The only off-balance-sheet lot control is 7,553 option lots from unnamed third-party sellers plus 3,013 lots through four 50/50 development JVs (two with Taylor Morrison, one with Hersh Family Investments, one Atlanta JV via The Providence Group). Room for a land banker is small by stated policy, but 2026 land spend was cut from $850M to $780M, cash fell to $100M and the revolver was drawn, so watch whether leadership's stance softens under the new Co-CEO (Jed Dolson) structure.
financing.land_strategy: Owns most (company framing: 'owning and self-developing land in desirable infill and infill-adjacent submarkets'). Targets entitled parcels that yield finished lots 12-24 months after purchase, also large multi-phase master plans of 5-10+ years that it says land bankers avoid; buying finished lots from third-party developers is a much smaller share. Explicitly does not use land banking. Target debt-to-capital about 20%. 2026 land budget: about $350M land/lot acquisition plus about $430M development (total $780M, cut from $850M).

financing.summary: Risewell Homes (legal issuer now Risewell Homes, Inc., formerly The New Home Company Inc.) is a private, Apollo-fund-owned builder that calls itself asset-light and funds itself with three tools: Apollo equity ($650M of new equity for the Landsea deal), Rule 144A senior unsecured notes (about $775M face across a 9.25% 2029 issue and an 8.5% 2030 issue) plus a $600M revolver, and land banking. Its one public land-bank relationship is with Kennedy Lewis / Millrose: a $700M commitment signed 2025-05-12, of which Millrose funded $494.5M net at the Landsea closing for 4,186 homesites optioned back to the builder. It controlled about 28,000 lots at the December 2025 rebrand, but no owned-versus-optioned split has been published since the Landsea take-private, because quarterly reports go only to registered bondholders. For a land banker the opening is that the Kennedy Lewis program covers only about 15% of the controlled lots, the unfunded part of the $700M (up to $100M of it for horizontal development) is not reported as drawn, and S&P rated the credit 'B' (CreditWatch positive) in 2025, so land-light capital is how this sponsor-owned builder grows.
financing.land_strategy: Asset-light in its own words: New Home described itself as a "diversified asset-light homebuilder" in the Landsea tender documents and on Risewell's investor page, and CEO Matthew Zaist told The Builder's Daily the thesis is to scale operations without owning more land than necessary. No published target for the share of lots optioned. Before the deal, Landsea (the larger half) controlled 55% of its 10,516 lots by option or purchase contract at 2025-03-31 and aimed for 3 to 4 years of supply on a 24 to 36 month development horizon.

lots.source_title: New Home Co. and Landsea Homes Unite Under New National Brand: Risewell Homes (company release via PRWeb, 2025-12-02)
lots.note: About 28,000 lots controlled (company's rounded figure), with 120+ actively selling communities in 11 markets across 7 states. No owned or optioned split is public since the take-private. Latest public split is Landsea alone at 2025-03-31: 4,710 owned, 5,806 controlled by option or purchase contract, 10,516 total (55.2% controlled, calculated); see https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1721386/000172138625000018/lhi-20250331.htm. At least 4,186 homesites are optioned from Millrose (Kennedy Lewis program) since 2025-06-25.

land_banking.description: Land bank commitment letter ('Project Lakeland') signed 2025-05-12: up to $700M, 100% provided by KLIM, with up to $600M funded at the Landsea closing and up to $100M for horizontal development afterwards. KLIM buys properties and grants homesite options (and construction agreements up to a guaranteed contract sum). Option terms run up to 72 months, and properties are grouped in pools of at least four projects with cross-termination and a $20M cap per pool on the builder's total payment obligation. Total takedown price must be at least 105.25% of the closing commitment. It was conditioned on at least $650M of sponsor equity. Fees (initial option fee, monthly option fee, termination fee, asset management fee, minimum project return) are in an unfiled fee letter.
land_banking.source_title: Land Bank Commitment Letter, KLIM to The New Home Company Inc., 2025-05-12 (Landsea Schedule TO Ex. (b)(1))
land_banking.note: Signed by Darren Richman for KLIM and Miek Harbur (EVP, General Counsel and Secretary) for New Home. Funding was placed with Millrose (next row). Neither the builder nor Millrose has published whether the remaining ~$205M of the commitment (including the $100M horizontal tranche) was drawn.

land_banking.description: At the Landsea closing on 2025-06-25 Millrose bought $522.8M of land (4,186 homesites), paying $494.5M in cash net of $28.3M of builder option deposits, and optioned the homesites back to New Home. Millrose's FY2025 10-K counts this as part of the up-to-$700M commitment, and its Q3 2026 deck lists New Home / Landsea as one of three builder M&A deals it has financed ($700M of land assets, 4,186 homesites).
land_banking.source_title: Millrose Properties FY2025 10-K, Note 3 Spin-Off and Other Significant Business Transactions
land_banking.note: Deposit equals about 5.4% of land value (calculated), well below the roughly 10.5% on Millrose's Lennar book. The homesites span five states (Cox Castle, Millrose counsel, 2025-07-21), and Millrose financed the purchase from a $1.0B Goldman-led delayed-draw term loan, since refinanced. Corroborated by https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2017206/000119312526432747/ck0002017206-ex99_2.htm (Millrose Q3 2026 deck).

profile.legal_name: Holding Company of The Villages, Inc.
markets: The Villages, Central Florida (Sumter, Lake and Marion counties)
profile.org_note: One family-owned master developer, not a divisional builder: there are no regions or division presidents. The Morse family (siblings Mark Morse, Tracy Morse and Jennifer Parr) owns a holding company whose affiliates hold the land and build the homes (public records name The Villages Land Company, LLC, The Villages Development Company, The Villages of Lake-Sumter, Inc. and Buffalo Hide and Cattle Company). Land and capital decisions sit with the family and the CEO, Robert Chandler IV, who ran development before his 2026 promotion; Martin Dzuro handles entitlements. No CFO or treasurer is publicly named.
profile.summary: Not a conventional production homebuilder: The Villages is a single, family-owned, age-restricted (55+) master-planned retirement community in Central Florida that develops its own land and builds and sells its own homes (about 83,400 units sold to date, more than 2,100 in 2026 through mid-October, average price just under $500,000, per an October 2026 bond roadshow reported by Bloomberg). The community covers about 57,000 acres, the family holds tens of thousands of undeveloped acres around it, and roads, utilities, golf and recreation are paid for by its community development districts selling tax-exempt special assessment bonds that homebuyers repay. It is an unlikely land-banking customer: it owns decades of land outright, does not buy finished lots from third parties, and already has cheap, non-recourse lot-development money through district bonds.

financing.summary: Not a conventional for-sale homebuilder: The Villages is a family-owned retirement-community developer that owns its future land outright and builds on its own lots, so it has no option or land-bank programme and none is publicly linked to it. Lot development is financed off its balance sheet through its own community development districts, which sell unrated tax-exempt special assessment bonds (underwritten by Jefferies and Morgan Stanley): $155.5 million and $163 million in District 15 (2023, 2024), $127 million in District 16 (November 2025) and almost $180 million more marketed in October 2026, with District 16 seeking court validation for up to $606.6 million. The developer fronts construction and is reimbursed from bond proceeds, and amenities are financed separately through investment-grade bonds backed by resident amenity fees. Company-level bank debt, cash and leverage are not public. The Morse family also raised liquidity by selling its Citizens First Bank to Seacoast in 2025 (about $711 million at announcement). Room for a land banker is small: the plausible openings are the non-age-restricted Middleton community, the Benderson partnerships, or a future ownership change, not the core business.
financing.land_strategy: Owns essentially all of its land, bought years ahead through family entities (The Villages Land Company, LLC, The Villages Development Company, Buffalo Hide and Cattle Company) and developed in-house; no stated owned-versus-optioned target and no evidence of third-party lot purchases. Florida Trend (Feb 2024) reported 26,000 acres owned in Wildwood alone, 18,700 of them undeveloped, plus a 3,200-acre Leesburg tract and 900 acres near Mascotte. The 57,000 acres often quoted is the whole community, most of it already built and sold.

financing.summary: Highland Homes is a private Texas builder, 100% employee-owned through an ESOP since 2016. It has no public debt, no SEC filings and no credit ratings, and its site says it is not driven by outside investors. It has historically bought finished lots from master-plan developers (Hillwood, Hines, Starwood Land, and the founders' own Sandbrock Ranch). Since 2025 it has also developed its own lots: 188 acres in Hines' Heritage Bend (Fulshear, 554 homes) and about 100 acres at Hillwood's Melina (Georgetown, about 400 homesites), led by Jeff Stinson (SVP of Land at the time; Chief Strategy and Land Officer since the August 2026 restructuring, bdmag.com 2026-08-06). Self-development puts more land on Highland's own balance sheet and needs horizontal capital. No land banker, lot-option financier, bank lender or credit facility has been publicly named, so a land banker would be a new relationship, not a replacement.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed and moving toward self-development. Highland has mainly bought finished lots from master-plan developers ('typically, when we purchase lots from a developer, all of the horizontal construction is complete', SVP Land Jeff Stinson, May 2025). Since 2025 it develops its own parcels inside third-party master plans, to time lot supply to demand, and says it is 'actively looking' for more such deals in Houston and across Texas. It has no published owned-vs-optioned target.

profile.org_note: Not a conventional homebuilder: HFHI is a 501(c)(3) umbrella (FY ends June 30; legal address Americus, GA; administrative HQ Atlanta) that supports independent, separately incorporated local affiliates, which buy the land, build the homes and hold the mortgages. HFHI itself has no land or division-president structure. The people who matter for land capital are the Chief Financial and Administration Officer (oversees Finance and Habitat Capital) and the head of Habitat Capital, the wholly owned CDFI that lends to affiliates for land acquisition, predevelopment and construction and runs the US Property Acquisition Fund; the SVP U.S. Office and Canada leads affiliate support.
profile.summary: Nonprofit, not a for-sale homebuilder: the Builder 100 closings are the combined output of independent local Habitat affiliates in all 50 states, each of which manages its own home-building, sources its own land and sells to lower-income buyers on affordable mortgages. HFHI in Atlanta is the support and funding hub (FY2026 revenue $393.7M, total assets $767.3M) and finances affiliates' land through its CDFI, Habitat Capital ($46.8M lent to 31 affiliates in 20 states in FY2026), and the $82.5M US Property Acquisition Fund managed by Enterprise Community Loan Fund. It is not a plausible lot-option / land-banking customer in the conventional sense: there is no central land buyer, no takedown schedule, and its land capital is concessionary (2% to 6% notes from banks and foundations).

financing.summary: Not a conventional for-sale homebuilder: Habitat for Humanity International (HFHI) is a nonprofit whose independent local affiliates buy land, build and sell the homes; HFHI itself holds no homebuilding land and has no lot-option programme. It is not a plausible land-banking customer in the conventional sense: there is no central land buyer or takedown pipeline, homes are sold at affordable prices to lower-income buyers, and land capital is philanthropic or concessionary. HFHI funds affiliates' land through its wholly owned CDFI, Habitat Capital ($46.8M lent to 31 affiliates in FY2026), and the US Property Acquisition Fund, an $82.5M vehicle launched March 2025 that borrows at 2% to 6.01% from JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Enterprise Community Loan Fund and foundations and on-lends to affiliates for land and property purchases. Consolidated borrowings were about $110M at June 30, 2026 ($57.1M notes payable, $52.9M investor notes backed by affiliate notes), against $767M of total assets. Any opening for a land banker would be one-off deals with individual large affiliates, or learning from the Property Acquisition Fund structure, not a corporate relationship with HFHI.
financing.land_strategy: HFHI owns no homebuilding land (land, buildings and equipment were $5.0M net at June 30, 2026). Each independent affiliate sources and holds its own land. HFHI supports them with acquisition, predevelopment and construction loans from Habitat Capital and the US Property Acquisition Fund, plus grants; there is no stated owned/optioned target and no lot-option structure.

land_banking.counterparty: US Property Acquisition Fund, LLC (HFHI subsidiary; fund manager Enterprise Community Loan Fund)
land_banking.description: In-house substitute for a land banker: an $82.5M fund run through Habitat Capital that lends to U.S. Habitat affiliates and mission-aligned entities to buy land and property. It is a loan fund, not a lot-option arrangement. Target is about 1,000 additional homes, a 5% lift on a 3,482-unit baseline.
land_banking.source_title: Habitat for Humanity International announces new partnership to invest $82.5 million in affordable housing
land_banking.note: Class A lenders: JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Enterprise Community Loan Fund. Class B: ImpactAssets, Arnold Ventures, Annie E. Casey Foundation, plus HFHI equity. Larson Foundation seed funding. The FY2026 audit caps fund borrowings at $72.5M and shows $52.1M drawn at June 30, 2026 (up from $24.2M a year earlier). A JPMorgan-sponsored Commercial Observer piece (2025-06-16) puts JPMorgan's commitment at $30M and the average projected home price at $300,000.

land_banking.counterparty: Habitat Capital, LLC (HFHI's wholly owned CDFI, formerly Habitat Mortgage Solutions)
land_banking.description: Lends to affiliates for land acquisition, predevelopment, construction, mini-perm, bridge and working capital, and runs New Markets Tax Credit allocations and a mortgage origination platform. FY2026: $46.8M closed in 33 loans to 31 affiliates in 20 states.

land_banking.note: Habitat Capital balance sheet per the annual report: total assets $153.3M, liabilities $123.2M, net assets $30.2M at FY2026. Loan volume by year: FY2023 $11.9M, FY2024 $30.9M, FY2025 $33.5M, FY2026 $46.8M. Example on the Habitat Capital page: a $1.85M acquisition loan to Austin Habitat for 30 home sites. An 'Enterprise Line of Credit' pilot gives multi-project financing to affiliates.

key_metrics.source_title: HFHI consolidated financial statements, June 30, 2026 and 2025 (audit report dated November 17, 2026, Grant Thornton)

gaps: Head of land acquisition / land development: none exists at HFHI. Land is bought, entitled and developed by the independent local affiliates, each with its own executive director and (at larger affiliates) real-estate staff; those people are not mapped here.

Current head of Habitat Capital: not publicly confirmed. The FY2026 Form 990 shows Daniel Gura's role ending February 2026 and a VP & Executive Director posting appeared in search results; no successor announcement found.
Staff treasurer / head of treasury at HFHI: not publicly disclosed (the board has a volunteer Treasurer, Mary Mack).
Habitat Capital 'Head of Lending & Programs' and 'Head of Strategy & Operations': roles were advertised (seen in search snippets); holders not publicly named.
Reporting lines below the CEO (who reports to the new COO versus the CEO) are not published, apart from the SVP International Operations reporting to the COO.

Leaders of the largest land-buying affiliates (for example Twin Cities, Charlotte Region, Metro Denver, Greater Los Angeles, Houston, Collier County) are outside this file's scope; they are the real land decision-makers.
Email pattern: not found in a public source; no direct phone numbers published for executives.
Web search allowance for the swarm ran out part-way through; conference-speaker and trade-press checks on Habitat Capital staff could not be completed.
Number of U.S. affiliates: not stated in the documents opened (a search snippet said more than 1,000; Habitat Capital's page says it has lent to more than 350 of them).

How to read the key metrics: Total debt = notes payable $57.1M + investor notes payable $52.9M (excludes leases and the $143.7M GGRF programme advance). Cash is unrestricted cash and equivalents ($58.2M a year earlier); a further $266.4M is restricted cash ($143.7M GGRF, $122.7M other) and $274.7M is investments. Liquidity is the audit's figure for financial assets available for general expenditure within one year ($119.4M a year earlier), before the undrawn $10M line. Total assets $767.3M, net assets $452.1M, FY2026 revenue $393.7M, expenses $382.9M. No public credit rating found.
Lot counts (owned, optioned, controlled): not published. Land sits with the independent affiliates and is not consolidated or reported at network level.

Named land banker or lot-option partner: none. No public link to Domain Real Estate Partners, Millrose Properties, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon appears in HFHI's FY2026 audit, annual report or fund releases; a wider press search could not be run because the swarm's web-search allowance was used up.
Investor notes payable ($52.9M): investors not named.
$10M line of credit: bank, pricing and covenants not disclosed.
$5.0M non-interest-bearing performance-based note: lender and maturity not disclosed.

US Property Acquisition Fund: loan terms to affiliates (rate, tenor, advance rate), number of loans made and acres or lots financed are not publicly disclosed. One example seen only in a search snippet: a $1.19M loan to Habitat Wake County for 4.5 acres (not confirmed on an opened page).
Habitat Capital's own funding lines (the $123.2M of liabilities on its stand-alone balance sheet) are not broken out by lender beyond what the consolidated audit shows.
Credit ratings: none found in the documents opened; SEC EDGAR was not checked (nonprofit, not an SEC registrant as far as the audit shows).
M&A: none found for HFHI in 2025 to 2026. It is a nonprofit federation and does not acquire builders; mergers between local affiliates happen but were not tracked.

Network-level financing (affiliates' own bank lines, bond issues, mortgage sales) is outside HFHI's statements. HFHI's release puts federated network revenue at about $3.4B for FY2026 against HFHI's own $393M.

U.S. new-home count for FY2026 is not stated in households in the documents opened: the annual report gives 16,364 individuals served by new and rehab construction in the U.S. and Canada, using a four-people-per-household conversion.

financing.summary: Adams Homes is a private, family-controlled builder with no SEC filings, no public notes and no ratings, so almost nothing about its balance sheet is disclosed. What the public record does show is a two-company model: the affiliated Pensacola lot developer Garden Street Communities Southeast, LLC buys and develops land and sells finished lots to Adams Homes in blocks (two 50-lot takedowns at $4.25M each were recorded in Jacksonville in June and October 2026), so Garden Street already does the job a land banker would do, inside the family. A county-records aggregator shows the money behind it is bank debt: Texas Capital Bank, Regions Bank, Synovus Bank and Wells Fargo Bank are the largest mortgagees of record on Adams Homes entities, and Centennial Bank recorded a $100.0M mortgage on Garden Street on 2026-05-05. No land banker, lot-option fund or joint-venture partner is publicly linked to either company, which means the opening for Domain is to supplement or replace bank-funded land held by Garden Street, and the people to reach are Bryan (William B.) Adams and the Garden Street land team.
financing.land_strategy: Not stated by the company; no owned/optioned target is published. In practice it is a captive-developer model: Garden Street Communities Southeast, LLC (founded 2016, same Pensacola building) acquires and develops land in about twenty Southeastern markets and sells finished lots to homebuilders, and recorded deeds show Adams Homes of Northwest Florida, Inc. buying those lots in 50-lot blocks. Adams Homes also buys single scattered lots directly in older platted Florida communities and runs a build-on-your-lot program in a few Florida divisions.

land_banking.description: Privately held residential lot developer founded in 2016 and headquartered at 100 W Garden St, Pensacola (Adams Homes is in the same building). It buys land, entitles and develops it, and sells finished single-family and townhome lots to homebuilders, aimed at entry-level, first move-up and active-adult product. It says it works in three regions and twenty markets across FL, GA, AL, NC, SC and TX; its locations page also lists Mississippi.

Garden Street's job postings (Nov 2026) call it one of the largest privately held residential land developers in the Southeast, operating in seven states.

land_banking.description: Adams Homes treats Garden Street staff as its own people: its 2025 Founder's Club awards (company blog, July 2026) include a Director of Land Development in Spring Hill credited for his work on 'the Garden Street team' and on significant deals. It publishes no financial statements, has no SEC filings and no public debt, so lot counts, bank lines, lenders and leverage are not public. What is public is the model: land is entitled and developed in-house by Grand Communities, and the chairman's stated focus is land development and banking relationships, which points to bank-funded, self-developed lots rather than third-party land banking. No public link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis, TPG Angelo Gordon or any other land banker was found. The opening for a land banker is growth outside the legacy footprint: Raleigh (entered 2025) and Lexington (entered 2026, first community about $40M) are markets where the company has no long-held land pipeline, and the only named lenders anywhere in the group (First Financial Bank and Associated Bank, on a $48M affiliate apartment construction loan) are regional banks.
