financing.summary: Until May 2026 United Homes Group (Great Southern Homes, Rosewood Communities; Columbia, SC) was a Nasdaq-listed, almost fully land-light builder: at 2025 year end it owned 284 lots and controlled 6,941 through lot option contracts (96%), with $40.5M of deposits against $270.6M of remaining option purchase price. Lots came from third-party developers, land developers affiliated with controlling holder Michael Nieri (Land to Lots, PC Land Development, Pennington Development) and land bank partners, including a $150M land fund agreed with Developers Capital Fund LLC in 2024 and a 'third party land bank' called GSH Land Fund, LLC. Corporate funding was a $220M Wells Fargo-agented secured construction revolver ($78.2M drawn) and a $70M subordinated term loan agented by Kennedy Lewis (SOFR + 675-775 bps); both needed covenant relief in Sept 2025 and March 2026 and were repaid and terminated when Stanley Martin (Daiwa House) closed its all-cash merger on 2026-05-04. UHG is now a wholly owned Stanley Martin subsidiary, so new land-bank capital would be decided and priced at the Stanley Martin/Daiwa level. Those parents have far more balance sheet than UHG had, which may reduce the need for outside land-bank capital in the South Carolina markets.
financing.land_strategy: Land-light, in the company's own words: it buys finished lots through lot option contracts with third-party developers, related-party developers and land bank partners, putting up deposits of typically 15-20% of the purchase price with staggered takedowns. On land bank contracts UHG usually pays development costs and is reimbursed the next month. At 2025-12-31, 96% of about 7,200 owned or controlled lots were controlled through options. In 2023 CEO Jack Micenko said UHG would not carry large owned lot inventories and would hold lots as options through Pennington, the Nieri-affiliated land business. No numeric target was stated. Post-merger strategy under Stanley Martin is not disclosed.

lots.note: Item 1 table by division (owned/controlled): Midlands 151/3,935; Coastal 59/1,499; Upstate 11/1,352; Rosewood 38/109; Raleigh 25/46. land_banking.description: Described in the merger information statement as the third-party land bank working on UHG's behalf. A December 2025 proposal from Nieri-affiliated developers asked UHG to direct the fund to sell common-area acreage and road access at the Halton Oaks community to one of those developers.

land_banking.note: Sponsor, size and lot count not disclosed. In September 2025 Stanley Martin's proposal also required third-party consents under UHG's 'land banking agreements', which confirms more than one such contract existed. The counterparties to those agreements are not named.

land_banking.counterparty: Unnamed third-party land banker (finished-lot sale and repurchase option)
land_banking.description: Starting in Q1 2024, UHG sold finished lots to a land banker and took options to buy them back. This is accounted for as a financing: the lots stay on the balance sheet as real estate inventory not owned, and the land banker funds about 80% of their carrying value. Q1 2024 proceeds were $14.2M, and inventory not owned was $17.8M at 2024-03-31.
land_banking.source_title: UHG Q1 2024 Form 10-Q (filed 2024-05-10)
land_banking.note: UHG's maximum exposure was $1.9M at 2024-12-31 and $0.2M at 2025-12-31 (FY2025 10-K Note 2, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830188/000183018826000009/R9.htm), so the program had nearly run off. In 2024 UHG also paid closing costs for a related party to move land to one of its land banking partners (FY2025 10-K Note 9).

land_banking.counterparty: PC Entities (Land to Lots, LLC; PC Land Development Co., LLC; Pennington Development, LLC)
land_banking.description: Land developers affiliated with controlling stockholder and former Executive Chairman Michael Nieri, with lot option contracts that historically supplied a large share of UHG's developed lots. Related-party lot deposits were $4.9M at 2025-12-31 (2024: $6.8M). The February 2026 'PC Property Agreements' sped up UHG's purchase of finished lots and raw land at Camellia Park, Palomino Oaks and Southbridge, added a new raw-land purchase at Winter Farms, and included the Halton Oaks acreage sale. The information statement says existing contract prices were reduced overall.
land_banking.source_title: UHG DEFM14C information statement (filed 2026-04-10)
land_banking.note: Entity names and the PC Property Agreements are from the DEFM14C. The $4.9M deposit figure is from FY2025 10-K Note 9 (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830188/000183018826000009/R17.htm). No lot counts or prices were disclosed for the PC properties. Nieri's restrictive covenants were narrowed in his February 2026 waiver, so these entities may stay active as South Carolina lot developers outside Stanley Martin.

land_banking.counterparty: All lot option counterparties combined (third-party developers, related parties, land bank partners)
land_banking.description: Aggregate lot option book: $40.5M of non-refundable deposits controlling 6,941 lots, with $270.6M of remaining purchase price at 2025-12-31 (2024: $48.2M deposits, $352.2M remaining). Counterparties are treated as unconsolidated VIEs. Forfeited deposits were under $0.1M in 2025.
land_banking.source_title: UHG FY2025 10-K Note 2, Variable Interest Entities (XBRL R9)
land_banking.note: amount_usd_m is the remaining aggregate purchase price under option contracts, not deposits.

ma.counterparty: Stanley Martin Homes, LLC (subsidiary of Daiwa House Industry)
ma.description: Merger agreement signed 2026-02-22 and announced 2026-02-23. Stanley Martin bought UHG for $1.18 per share in cash, an enterprise value of about $221M (about $99.3M of equity per the information statement). The deal had no financing condition; Stanley Martin used cash on hand. Nieri holders with about 70% of the vote approved it by written consent. It closed 2026-05-04 through Union MergeCo, Inc. UHG was delisted from Nasdaq and deregistered (Form 15, 2026-05-14). All bank and term debt was repaid at closing.
ma.map_impact: United Homes Group (#56, 1,192 closings in 2025) is now a wholly owned subsidiary of Stanley Martin (#18), owned by Daiwa House. It adds about 7,200 controlled lots in the Columbia (Midlands), Greenville/Spartanburg (Upstate) and Myrtle Beach (Coastal) markets of South Carolina, plus Augusta, GA and Raleigh, NC, to Stanley Martin. The UHG executive officers (CEO Jack Micenko, Executive Chairman Michael Nieri, Keith Feldman, Tom O'Grady, Robert Penny, Jeremy Pyle, Shelton Twine) ceased to be officers at closing; CFO Randy Kotler signed the closing 8-K. Land and capital decisions now sit with Stanley Martin and Daiwa.
ma.source_title: UHG 8-K filed 2026-05-04 (completion of merger with Stanley Martin; Item 1.02 termination of credit agreements)
ma.note: Enterprise value from the 2026-02-23 joint press release (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830188/000110465926018344/tm266691d1_ex99-1.htm); equity figure and funding from the DEFM14C (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830188/000114036126014128/ny20067664x2_defm14c.htm). Advisors: Vestra Advisors and Paul, Weiss (UHG special committee); Maynard Nexsen (Stanley Martin). Termination fee $4M each way.

ma.counterparty: None (strategic review; bidders included Stanley Martin Holdings and unnamed Parties A, B, C and F)
ma.description: The special committee formed in March 2025 (review announced 2025-05-19) contacted 38 buyers; 22 signed NDAs. First-round bids: Stanley Martin $150M all cash, Party A $100-120M, Party C $250M in cash and stock. Only Stanley Martin bid in round two ($134M, August 2025), then cut its bid to $121M, $85M and $94M. The committee ended the review on 2025-10-20 and chose to stay independent. Six directors then resigned: four (Enoch, Pirrello, Levine, Dozier) because Nieri would not give up the Executive Chairman role, and two (Haley, Clements) citing other commitments. Talks with Stanley Martin resumed and produced the February 2026 deal. Party F offered about $66M of equity value in November 2025 and was rejected.
ma.map_impact: No ownership change at the time. It shows the falling valuation and covenant pressure that led to the Stanley Martin sale. Party C, an unnamed strategic buyer, had looked at a deal involving one of UHG's existing lenders.
ma.source_title: UHG DEFM14C information statement (filed 2026-04-10)
ma.note: Review conclusion and director resignations: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830188/000110465925100651/tm2529074d1_8k.htm. Verifier 2026-11-19: corrected 'six directors resigned after Nieri refused to step down' to four for that reason plus two citing other commitments, per that 8-K.

industry_deals.description: Closed 2026-05-04 (announced 2026-02-23; merger agreement dated 2026-02-22). Stanley Martin acquired Nasdaq-listed United Homes Group by merger for $1.18 per share in cash, an enterprise value of about $221 million; the stock and warrants were delisted. The executive officers listed in the closing 8-K, including chief executive Jack Micenko and executive chairman Michael Nieri, ceased to be officers at closing.
industry_deals.map_impact: United Homes Group (#56, 1,192 closings in the ranking) is now a wholly owned subsidiary of Stanley Martin (#18): the two rows share one owner, Daiwa House. United Homes' top leadership left at closing. Adds Greenville, Spartanburg, Clemson, Columbia and Myrtle Beach, South Carolina and Augusta, Georgia to Stanley Martin (per HousingWire).
industry_deals.source_title: United Homes Group 8-K filed 2026-05-04 (completion of merger with Stanley Martin Homes)

In October 2025 the committee concluded the company should stay independent given market conditions; four independent directors then said they would resign after controlling stockholder and executive chairman Michael Nieri declined to step down from that role, and two other directors also resigned.
industry_deals.map_impact: No map change at the time: United Homes Group (#56) stayed independent. It set up the February 2026 agreement to sell to Stanley Martin at $1.18 per share.

Homebuilding runs through two Homes by WestBay divisions (North and South) plus the Casa Fresca Homes subsidiary; land is bought and developed centrally through HBWB Development under Mark Metheny, and finance sits with Beth Bradburn (COO, former CFO), an incoming CFO whose name is not public, and a treasurer. profile.summary: Conventional for-sale homebuilder: Tampa Bay's largest locally owned private builder, founded in 2009 and led by founder Willy Nunn, with about 1,150 to 1,200 closings a year and roughly $700M of sales across move-up homes (Homes by WestBay) and entry-level homes (Casa Fresca). It builds in about 20 communities in five Florida counties and reports 11,490 owned or controlled lots, close to ten years of supply. It develops much of its own land, including four master-planned communities, and has started multifamily and build-to-rent lines, so it is a plausible land-banking customer.

financing.summary: Private, founder-led company with no public debt or SEC filings found, so its bank lines and land loans are not disclosed. It is a land-heavy self-developer: it reports 11,490 owned or controlled lots (close to ten years of supply at about 1,155 closings), develops its own master-planned communities through HBWB Development, and also buys finished lots from outside developers. The one named outside capital partner is GTIS Partners, which formed a $50M equity joint venture with the Casa Fresca subsidiary in 2021; the founder has also referred to unnamed 'capital partners'. No public link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. A long owned pipeline, growth into new counties and new build-to-rent and multifamily lines, plus a leadership and CFO handover through 2027, suggest real room for a land banker, but nothing public shows it using one today.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed, leaning toward owning and developing its own land. The company describes itself as a developer and homebuilder: it has put nearly $96M into large land purchases and is developing four master-planned communities (Hawkstone, Crosswind Ranch, Pasadena Ridge, Mitchell Falls), while also buying homesites in third-party communities such as Verona, Wellen Park, Lakewood Ranch and Waterset. No stated owned-versus-optioned target.

profile.summary: NOT a conventional for-sale homebuilder. This is the Scottsdale, Arizona company at lifestylehomesaz.com (founded 2009 by Lance Keller), a fee-based general contractor that builds build-to-rent (single-family rental) communities for developers and investors; it is unrelated to the Lifestyle Homes companies in Florida, California and elsewhere. Every project on its site is in Arizona (it is also licensed in Nevada and says it serves Texas); a December 2025 trade article put it at about 25 communities and 4,800+ rental homes built, with 14 communities under construction. Its Builder 100 'closings' are rental homes delivered to clients, which explains the low revenue per home. It does not buy or hold lots, so it is not a direct land-banking customer; land decisions sit with its developer clients (Empire Group of Companies has 15 of the 24 projects on its list).

financing.summary: NOT a conventional for-sale homebuilder and not a direct land-banking customer. Lifestyle Homes (Scottsdale, AZ) is a privately owned, fee-based general contractor that builds build-to-rent communities on land owned and financed by its developer and investor clients, so it carries no lot inventory of its own that a land banker could take out. Its own funding (owner equity, any working-capital line, bonding) is not publicly disclosed; the only public hint is a conference listing saying it has been vetted by leading lenders. The financing that matters sits with its clients: Empire Group of Companies (15 of 24 listed projects), plus GTIS Partners, Dominium, El Dorado Holdings, Moderne Communities, Zen Investing and Higher Ground Developments. For Domain the value of this account is as a route to those build-to-rent land owners, not as a lot-option counterparty.
financing.land_strategy: Owns no land by design. The company says it began in 2009 buying raw land and finished lots for small infill for-sale communities, then moved to fee-based general contracting for build-to-rent communities; clients bring the land.

land_banking.description: Largest client by far: named as the developer on 15 of the 24 build-to-rent communities on Lifestyle Homes' project list (the 'Village at ...' series across metro Phoenix and Pinal County). profile.org_note: Single-entity, family-owned builder run from one home office in College Station; no division presidents are published, and the CEO told HousingWire (2026-10-27) that divisional leadership is the next organisational step under consideration. Land (acquisition, entitlement, design, development) sits with one executive, VP of Development & Acquisition Stephen Grove; finance sits with CFO Jason Williams; both are presumed to report to owner/CEO Doug French. Legal name per Texas TDLR record and BBB profile (incorporated 1987).
profile.summary: Private, second-generation family-owned entry-level builder (attached and detached, roughly low $200Ks to high $400Ks) in secondary Texas markets: Bryan/College Station, Waco, Temple/Killeen, Georgetown/Jarrell, Seguin, Huntsville/Conroe and Tyler. It deliberately avoids the big metros (exited Houston around 2023-2024) and is exiting one more underperforming market in 2026. HousingWire reports 973 sales for about $310M in 2025 (Builder 100: 1,068 closings) and guidance of 1,100-1,200 sales in 2026; a build-for-rent arm (South Six Construction Group) is under 10% of deliveries. Conventional for-sale builder that entitles and develops its own lots, so a plausible but small land-banking customer.

financing.summary: Westin Homes is a conventional private for-sale builder, wholly controlled by founder Jason Golan, with no public debt, no SEC filings and no disclosed lenders, lot counts or capital partners. Its land model is asset-light by habit: it builds on finished lots bought from third-party master-plan developers (Johnson Development, Hines, Hillwood, Ashton Gray and others) in 41 communities across Houston and Austin, so developers already carry most of its land. No land banker, lot-option financier or outside investor is named anywhere public, and nothing links it to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon. It is a plausible but modest land-banking customer: the opening is finished-lot takedown financing inside developer communities, and the builder-partner land purchases with Hines (Fulshear, 2025) show it will commit to land ahead of lot delivery.

financing.summary: Empire Homes is a conventional for-sale homebuilder (entry-level and move-up, plus Ontario condos), privately owned by the Guizzetti family through Willowdale Asset Management in Vaughan, Ontario. It funds itself with high-yield bonds issued by Empire Communities Corp. (US$475 million of 9.75% senior notes due 2029 and C$225 million of 7.625% senior unsecured notes due November 2029), a revolving credit facility whose size and lenders are not public, and family equity; S&P had the issuer on negative outlook in January 2026. It carries a large land position on its own and its affiliates' books (more than 28,000 potential future homesites) and develops lots in-house through sister company Precedent Land Company. No outside land banker or lot-option partner is named publicly. It is a plausible land-banking customer for its U.S. Sunbelt divisions, given the cost of its unsecured debt and the negative outlook, but note that its parent also owns Rooftop Capital, which sells lot banking and A&D loans to other U.S. builders, so the group understands the product and competes at the small end.
financing.land_strategy: Land-heavy and vertically integrated, in its own words 'fully vertically integrated': it buys and develops land itself (the former land division, now Precedent Land Company, a sister company under Willowdale) and cites a strategic land position of more than 28,000 potential future homesites in planning, development or construction. No owned versus optioned split or land-light target is published.

Earlier company figures: more than 25,000 (Nov 2024), more than 27,000 (Feb 2025), more than 29,000 (Jul 2025). Years of supply not computed because the homesite count is not U.S.-only.

financing.summary: Conventional for-sale builder, so in principle a land-banking customer, but its capital picture changed on 30 July 2026: the employee-owned (ESOP) company was sold in full to Stanley Martin Homes, a Daiwa House Group subsidiary, and is now a wholly owned subsidiary. Nothing about Holiday's own debt, lenders or facilities has ever been public, and no land banker or lot-option financier is named anywhere for it. Its land model was capital-light by design: scattered lots bought close to the start of construction, finished lots taken down from third-party developers, and, since 2024, a growing share of communities it develops itself. It brought about 10,600 controlled lots to Stanley Martin (owned versus optioned split not disclosed). Funding now most likely flows from Stanley Martin and Daiwa House, whose management is reported to be targeting roughly 100,000 controlled US lots, so the land-banking conversation runs through Reston and the parent as much as through Melbourne.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed and capital-light. HousingWire's July 2026 coverage, quoting the company's advisor Zelman Partners, describes scattered-lot buying with 'real-time' lot absorption (and roughly 65-day build cycles) as an asset-light model. The company itself says it buys lots inside existing developments and, increasingly, buys tracts and develops whole communities (Huntington Park in Titusville, Citrus Ridge in Lake Wales, Mallard Landing in Okeechobee, two Brevard County communities); in 2024 leadership set a goal of expanding land acquisitions. No stated owned/optioned target.

financing.summary: First Texas Homes is a conventional private for-sale builder controlled by one individual (Randall Van Wolfswinkel is the only officer and director on the 2026 Texas state record), with no public debt, no SEC filings and no lender, land banker or capital partner named anywhere public. The one hard data point on how it handles land is a 2021 municipal bond offering document for Legacy Hills in Celina: First Texas Homes, Inc. bought a 132-acre pod from the Centurion American master developer for about $12.0M in cash and planned to develop 490 lots itself in three phases through about 2030, with roughly $21.1M of internal infrastructure to be funded with cash or loans as needed. That points to a builder that puts raw land and development spend on its own balance sheet in at least some communities, alongside finished-lot purchases in other developers' master plans. It is a plausible land-banking customer (the later Legacy Hills phases are exactly the kind of self-developed sections a land banker finances), but there is no public sign that it uses one today, and its owner-funded, cash-buying profile may mean limited appetite.

It was to build the lots itself: 490 lots in three phases (163 / 163 / 164), with phase starts projected for Q1 2022, Q3 2024 and Q4 2026 and final home sales in Q2 2030, and about $21.07M of water, sewer, drainage, landscaping and roads to be funded with cash or loans as necessary. Its rights to district reimbursement for those improvements were assigned to the master developer.

financing.summary: Ivory Homes is a conventional for-sale homebuilder and a plausible land-banking customer on paper, but a hard one in practice: it is family-owned, land-heavy by choice and appears to fund land from its own balance sheet. The company says about a third of earnings go to community giving and the rest is reinvested in future neighborhoods, and its November 2026 deck reports 20,548 lots owned or controlled across Utah (roughly 20 years at 2025 closings of 1,028, my arithmetic) and $162M put into new land and lots in 2026. Land is held and entitled through the affiliated Ivory Development, LLC and through partnerships with long-time landowners (Hoytsville with Larry H. Miller Communities; Browns Canyon for the Garff and Rogers families). No land banker, lot-option financier, bank lender, credit facility or outside equity partner is named in any source opened in this run, and the sister ICO Companies says its principals invest their own capital and manage surplus cash across the combined businesses. The opening for a land banker, if any, is the sheer size and duration of the land position (large master plans of 2,000+ lots) rather than a visible funding need.
financing.land_strategy: Owns or controls a very long land position and develops its own lots: the Ivory family 'began by developing land' and the affiliated Ivory Development acquires, entitles and plats land ahead of home production. The company frames this as reinvesting retained earnings in 'future neighborhoods' and staying local and family-owned rather than selling to a larger group. No stated land-light target; the owned versus optioned split is not disclosed.

financing.summary: McGuinn is a conventional for-sale entry-level builder that also sells homes in bulk to build-to-rent investors, so it is not a nonprofit or pure BTR operator. Before its sale it financed growth through two recapitalisations: a 2021 deal advised by Builder Advisor Group that moved its assets onto 100% non-recourse debt and paid the founder out, and a 2024 reorganisation with unnamed 'long-term capital providers' (described as a family-office private-equity partner), advised by Whelan Advisory; no lender, land banker or lot-option partner was ever named. In July 2026 Mungo Homes (Clayton Home Building Group, Berkshire Hathaway) announced it had acquired McGuinn, and Mungo is joining Taylor Morrison in 2027, so McGuinn's land and capital now come from Berkshire's balance sheet. As a stand-alone land-banking customer it is effectively gone; any opportunity runs through Clayton / Taylor Morrison.
financing.land_strategy: Not stated as land-light or land-heavy. The company targets cheaper 'F lots' farther from job centres to keep homes under $300,000, and it buys finished or in-progress communities from other builders (an August 2025 asset acquisition of several Columbia communities from a local builder, framed as securing lots for near-term deliveries). Owned versus optioned mix not disclosed.

financing.summary: Trumark is a private developer-builder that has been a consolidated subsidiary of Japan's Daiwa House Industry since 2020, when Daiwa House USA Inc. bought 60% from the two founders' family trusts and committed to further capital contributions. Before that it raised project-level money from institutional investors; since the deal it funds land from its own (Daiwa-backed) balance sheet, and its 2025 and 2026 releases announce roughly 2,000 lots and homesites as purchased, acquired or secured, with no mention of options. It has no public notes, no ratings and no disclosed credit-facility terms, and no land banker or lot-option financier is named in any public source found. The opening for a land banker is at the parent: Daiwa's debt-to-equity ratio reached 1.25 times in September 2026 against an earlier target of about 0.6, and its management told analysts the group may reduce interest-bearing debt and will balance investment with recovery over the next three to four years, while Trumark is trying to grow from 991 closings in 2025 into a fifth division in Washington.
financing.land_strategy: Owns and develops most of its land. Trumark describes itself as specialising in new residential land development, and Daiwa describes it as handling every stage from land development to housing supply. Its affiliate Trumark Communities (started 2013) is a master-planned community developer. Daiwa said in 2020 that Trumark would shift from institutional-investor project funding to using its own funds. No stated owned versus optioned target.

land_banking.counterparty: Daiwa House Industry Co., Ltd. (through Daiwa House USA Inc.)
land_banking.description: Parent and main capital source. Daiwa House USA agreed in January 2020 to buy 60% of Trumark Companies LLC and to make additional capital contributions to fund the business; Trumark's 2026 releases still name Daiwa as majority stakeholder and source of financial support. This is parent equity and backing, not a lot-option programme.
land_banking.source_title: Daiwa House news release: Notice Regarding Purchase of Equity Interests of Trumark Companies LLC (16 Jan 2020)
land_banking.note: Sellers were family trusts of Michael Maples and Gregg Nelson (50% each before the deal); expected transfer date 1 Feb 2020. The same release says Trumark had been procuring project funds from institutional investors (not named) and would shift to using its own funds. Amounts of capital contributed since are not disclosed. The Orange County Business Journal (23 Mar 2026) still describes the stake as 60%; no later change was found.

land_banking.counterparty: Master-plan land sellers (not named in the releases)
land_banking.description: Trumark buys lots inside third-party master plans as well as stand-alone sites. Announced in 2025 and 2026: 37 more lots at Sterling Ranch (Littleton, CO), described as acquired; 85 homes at Andara at the Great Park (Irvine) and 90 at Sunflower at Rienda in Rancho Mission Viejo, described as secured; and plans for 195 homes at The Trails in Bishop Ranch (San Ramon), where the release does not say whether the land is owned or under contract. No release names sellers, prices or any option or phased-takedown structure.
land_banking.source_title: Trumark Homes Expanding Southern California Footprint in 2026 (27 Jan 2026)
land_banking.note: Lot count is the sum of the four master-plan deals named (37 + 85 + 90 + 195). Sterling Ranch and Bishop Ranch details are in Trumark's releases of 12 Dec 2025 and 27 Aug 2026 (see capital_events). Whether any of these are rolling-option takedowns is not public. Verifier 2026-11-19: description corrected; the 27 Aug 2026 Bishop Ranch release announces plans to build and does not say the site was acquired or secured (earlier text said all four were acquired or secured). The cited 27 Jan 2026 source states only the Great Park and Rienda counts.

profile.summary: Conventional private for-sale builder (entry-level and move-up, about 1,000 closings a year) based in Portage, MI, calling itself Michigan's largest home builder: 100+ active communities across Michigan, northern Indiana and northwest Ohio, many in small towns, with 150+ move-in-ready spec homes on offer. It buys land directly from owners and cities (0.25 to 100 acres) and develops it in-house; a plausible but small-ticket land-banking customer, with many scattered positions rather than large master-planned takedowns.

financing.summary: Allen Edwin is a conventional private for-sale builder (with a build-to-lease side brand, Copper Bay) and has no public debt, no SEC filings and no published lot counts, lenders or capital partners. It buys land directly from landowners and municipalities (0.25 to 100 acres, plus scattered infill lots), develops it with an in-house land team, and carries 150+ spec homes, so land and inventory appear to sit on its own balance sheet funded by undisclosed private financing. The visible outside capital is public: Michigan housing TIF (brownfield) reimbursements and PILOT tax deals for its Workforce Housing projects, which the developer front-funds itself and recovers over 20 to 25 years. No land banker, lot-option financier or joint venture is named anywhere public, and the one option structure found is a phased purchase option granted by a city. It is a plausible land-banking customer in principle (about 1,000 closings a year, self-developed lots, a stated plan to add 250 homes a year), but ticket sizes are small and spread over 100+ mostly small-town communities, and part of the pipeline is held as rentals.
financing.land_strategy: Not stated by the company. Evidence points to owning and self-developing: a direct land-buying programme (single lots up to 100+ acres in MI, IN and OH), in-house land development and land planning/engineering staff, and phased purchases of municipal land under seller options. No land-light target or optioned-lot share is published.

financing.summary: Hakes Brothers is a conventional for-sale homebuilder, privately held by the founding family, with no SEC filings, no rated or public debt, and no announced land banker, lot-option financier, joint venture or outside capital partner. Nothing about its bank lines, lenders or balance sheet is public. What is visible is a builder that buys lots market by market, often finished lots from local developers and inside third-party master plans, and that has grown from about 730 closings in 2023 to the low 900s while opening three new markets (Kansas City, the Rio Grande Valley, the Austin area) in roughly three years. That pace on a family balance sheet, with 57 communities listed and eight more in pre-sale, makes it a plausible land-banking customer, but there is no public sign that it has used one, so the first call is a discovery call with the CFO (Andrew Vieth, ex-Beazer and Pulte finance) and the owners.
financing.land_strategy: Not stated by the company. Public evidence points to a mixed, lot-purchase model: in early 2022 its Rio Grande division president said it was buying lots around Socorro (El Paso) and weighing a 2,300-lot master-planned community near Santa Teresa, NM that was not yet signed; in Rio Rancho in 2024 it built on 44 lots in a subdivision delivered by a third-party developer; and in a 2026 Albuquerque home-show segment its representative said it has home sites in hand and plans to acquire more over the next few years. Many communities carry master-plan names (La Cima, Rancho Santa Teresa, Metro Verde, Mariposa), which suggests lot purchases from master developers rather than self-development. No owned versus optioned split or target is published.

land_banking.counterparty: Pierre Amestoy (developer of Los Diamantes, Rio Rancho, NM)
land_banking.description: Local developer delivered the Los Diamantes subdivision on land assembled by investors (Mike Skolnick and John Lewis are named); Hakes Brothers is the builder on 44 lots there for spec homes. This is a finished-lot supply relationship, not a land-bank facility, and the purchase terms (bulk or rolling takedown) are not disclosed.
land_banking.source_title: Albuquerque Journal: New luxury neighborhood is ready in Rio Rancho
land_banking.note: Included to show how the builder sources lots; it is not evidence of land banking.

profile.summary: Private, family-owned Mid-Atlantic and Southeast residential company founded in 1966; nearly 500 employees. For-sale homebuilding is only in Virginia (Richmond) and North Carolina (Raleigh, Southern Pines, Wilmington): the company site reports 580 homes closed in 2025 (430 VA, 150 NC), fewer than the Builder 100 figure. It is not a pure homebuilder: it also develops its own master-planned communities and owns and manages about 8,885 apartments in 27 communities across MD, VA, TN, NC, SC and GA; it sold its senior-living division in 2022. financing.summary: HHHunt is a private, family-owned, diversified residential company, not a pure for-sale homebuilder: it builds homes in Virginia and North Carolina (580 closed in 2025 per its own site), develops its own master-planned communities around Richmond through HHHunt Communities, and owns and manages about 8,885 apartments in 27 communities that it describes as income-producing ballast. Nothing public shows a land banker, lot-option financier or outside equity partner on the for-sale side; lots come from its own land-development arm and from finished-lot purchases negotiated by a four-person land acquisition team. The only named financing in public sources is property-level apartment debt (HUD-insured construction loans arranged by Berkadia, and a 2022 ACRE debt-fund acquisition loan). Corporate credit facilities, homebuilding lot lines and balance-sheet figures are not disclosed. It is a plausible but small land-banking customer: the opening is finished-lot or takedown structures for HHHunt Homes in Raleigh and Wilmington, where it has no in-house master-plan pipeline, and the finance relationship passes from Ann Kelly to Steve Brant on 2027-07-01.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed, leaning owner-developer. In Richmond it assembles and entitles tracts itself and develops master-planned communities (Edgebrook: 45 acres, 387 townhomes; The Aire: about 2,200 homes; River Mill: about 1,000 homes) in which HHHunt Homes builds. Elsewhere the land team buys finished lots for homebuilding and sites for apartments. The company tells land sellers it is privately held, diversified and long-term, and that it is actively looking for land in the Southeast. No stated owned-versus-optioned target.

profile.org_note: Small, centrally run private builder: a CEO (Joe Harris) and a short corporate team in Joplin over four market areas (Joplin metro, Springfield, Northwest Arkansas, Northeast Oklahoma); no published leadership page. Land appears to sit with co-founder Dan Mitchell and an affiliated Joplin developer, Land Development Group (unconfirmed title), and finance with the CFO; the company has been 100% owned by an employee stock ownership plan since 2020.
profile.summary: Faith-based, 100% employee-owned (ESOP, public benefit corporation since 2020) entry-level and move-up builder founded in Joplin after the 2011 tornado; it passed 5,000 homes sold in mid-2026, has about 230 employees and builds in southwest Missouri, Springfield MO, Northwest Arkansas and the Tulsa area. It already uses TPG Angelo Gordon's Essential Housing for finished-lot land banking in Northwest Arkansas (three recorded option deals, Dec 2025 to Oct 2026) and buys finished lots from third-party developers such as Calara, so it is a live land-banking customer with a competitor already in the account.

financing.summary: Private, 100% ESOP-owned builder with no public debt, ratings or financial statements, so almost all of its capital structure is not publicly disclosed. What county records (as reported by Talk Business) show is a three-part land model in Northwest Arkansas: land banking of finished lots with TPG Angelo Gordon's Essential Housing (three recorded two-year option deals from Dec 2025 to Oct 2026 covering 248 lots and about $22.2M), finished lots bought or contracted from third-party developers (Calara, Kinney Creek, Three Pistols, Saddle Hill Estates), and raw land or lot purchases funded with short local bank loans (First National Bank of Fort Smith, North American Savings Bank, earlier City Bank of Lubbock). It also moves small batches of completed homes into a wholly owned rental affiliate, Steppingstone Home Rentals LLC, financed by Arvest Bank. A competitor is already the incumbent land banker, but only Northwest Arkansas deals are visible; Springfield, Joplin and the new Tulsa market show no public land-bank activity, which is where room for a second provider is most plausible.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed and shifting land-lighter. In 2020 the company was described as self-developing most of its lots (buying raw land, entitling it and installing infrastructure), for example the 400-lot Orchard Park subdivision in Centerton. Since late 2025 it has added finished-lot option agreements with Essential Housing and a developer partnership with Calara, while still buying raw land outright (62.85 acres in Gravette, Oct 2026). No stated owned/optioned target.

profile.org_note: Family-owned and founder-led: Pat Neal (Founder & Chairman, owner) sits above a president (Douglas Miller, added about August 2026), a CFO (Nancy Reynolds) and an Executive VP of Land & Strategy (Jason Frost). Homebuilding is split into a North Division (Manatee/Sarasota) and a South Region (Lee/Collier, Tim Oak), with three brands: Neal Communities, Neal Signature Homes (luxury) and SimplyDwell Homes (attainable). Land decisions run through Pat Neal and Jason Frost; finance through Nancy Reynolds and Pamela Curran. Family affiliates sit alongside: Neal Land & Neighborhoods (John Neal, master-planned land developer) and a second land development company run by Michael Neal.
profile.summary: Private, family-owned Southwest Florida builder (founded 1970, about 27,000 homes built) selling in Manatee, Sarasota, Lee and Collier counties under Neal Communities, Neal Signature Homes and SimplyDwell Homes; headquarters at 5800 Lakewood Ranch Blvd N. It is a conventional for-sale homebuilder that buys and develops its own land: the company says it purchases the land it develops, and the founder says he is holding cash to buy more land, so it behaves more like a land owner than a land-light builder. Revenue fell to about $586M in 2025 from about $800M in 2024 (Business Observer), and a new president appeared on the leadership page around August 2026.

financing.summary: Neal Communities is a conventional for-sale homebuilder, privately owned by founder Pat Neal, and it publishes no financial statements, lot counts, lenders or facilities. What is public points to a self-funded, land-heavy model: the company says it purchases the land it develops, a 2024 Business Observer profile credits it with an aversion to debt, and in November 2025 Pat Neal said he is holding cash to buy land and expects to go further into the land business as other builders give up positions. Infrastructure is financed where possible through special district (CDD / stewardship district) municipal bonds, which he has said cost less than bank development loans, and raw land is typically tied up under long contracts with the sellers and closed only once permits are in hand (the $34.1M, 788-acre Alva purchase closed in August 2026 after about four years). No land banker, lot-option financier or outside capital partner is named anywhere public. As a land-banking customer it is plausible but not an obvious one: the owner prefers to own land and has cash, yet 2025 revenue fell about 27% to roughly $586M, he rated 2025 margins 3 out of 10, a new president arrived around August 2026, and large new positions (Alva, Boca Royale at Wellen Park, Kingston, Burnt Store Road) all need development capital.
financing.land_strategy: Owns and develops most of its own land, by choice. Company wording: 'we purchase the land we develop, build and sell the homes'. Founder's framing (November 2025): 'I'm a land guy', holding cash to buy land, will 'go more in the land business', and notes that the stock market penalises public builders for holding land. It also builds inside third-party master plans (Lakewood Ranch, Wellen Park, Kingston by Cameratta Companies) and in North River Ranch, developed by the family affiliate Neal Land & Neighborhoods. No stated owned/optioned target.

land_banking.description: Separate Neal family company run by John Neal (Pat Neal's son): a master-planned community developer whose flagship North River Ranch in Parrish is approved for 6,000 residences. It partners with Neal Communities on some projects (Neal Communities sells homes at Wildleaf at North River Ranch) and sells land to other builders; it is a family source of developed land rather than a land banker.

profile.summary: NOT a conventional for-sale homebuilder. NeighborWorks America is a congressionally chartered national nonprofit (Neighborhood Reinvestment Corporation, Washington, DC) that gives federal grant money, training and oversight to a network of 248 independent local nonprofits; its Builder 100 entry (No. 72 in 2026) simply adds up the for-sale homes those members built and sold. It owns no land, controls no lots and has no land or capital-markets staff, so it is not a plausible land-banking customer itself; any lot deal would be with an individual member nonprofit, and those are small, subsidy-driven and already served by two affiliated nonprofit lenders (Community Housing Capital and NeighborWorks Capital).

financing.summary: NOT a conventional for-sale homebuilder, and not a plausible land-banking customer. NeighborWorks America is a federally chartered nonprofit funded almost entirely by an annual congressional appropriation ($158 million core in fiscal 2025; total revenue $179 million; total assets only $68 million). It does not buy land, hold lots, borrow to build or sell homes: it passes grants to 248 independent local nonprofits, and those members built and sold the homes counted in the Builder 100 (875 closings in 2025). Land and construction money for the members comes from grants, local subsidy and two affiliated nonprofit lenders, Community Housing Capital and NeighborWorks Capital, which lend only or mainly to the network (land acquisition, predevelopment, construction; $169 million lent in fiscal 2024). The room for a commercial land banker is close to nil at the national level; at most a few of the largest member nonprofits could be one-off lot-option counterparties, and they would compare the price with subsidised nonprofit loans. Funding risk is real: the President's fiscal 2026 budget proposed ending the appropriation.
financing.land_strategy: None of its own. NeighborWorks America owns no development land and controls no lots; each member nonprofit sources its own sites (often donated, public or infill parcels, or community land trust land) with grant money, local subsidy and loans from the two affiliated capital corporations. The company's own framing is an 'intermediary' that supplies flexible, early-stage 'risk capital' grants that members can use for acquisition, predevelopment and development.

land_banking.description: National nonprofit loan fund (CDFI) in Silver Spring, MD, serving NeighborWorks member organisations. Lends for acquisition of vacant land or existing property (typically up to $10 to 15 million), predevelopment (up to $3 million, can revolve), construction including single-family (up to $20 million), mini-perm, permanent and enterprise loans. This is the network's nearest equivalent to land finance, at nonprofit pricing.
land_banking.source_title: NeighborWorks Capital website (home and Loan Capital pages)
land_banking.note: Amount is the permanent equity capital NeighborWorks America has put into NeighborWorks Capital (over $43 million, plus operating support), per its site; it says it has provided over $600 million of funding in total (undated). Operates independently but 'in strategic alignment' with NeighborWorks America. Leaders per its staff page: Jim Peffley, Chief Executive Officer (since 2022); Nancy Wagner-Hislip, Executive Vice President running lending, credit and portfolio (named July 2026); Matt Glatting, Chief Financial Officer; Ben Greenberg, Chief Lending & Customer Engagement Officer; Beth O'Leary, Chief Risk Officer. Not a land banker and no lot-option structure.

land_banking.description: National nonprofit lender (CDFI) in Decatur, GA, that describes itself as financing exclusively NeighborWorks America organisations. Products include lines of credit for early-stage costs, acquisition loans for vacant land and existing properties, single-family and multifamily construction, bridge, permanent, forward commitments and a warehouse line for nonprofit mortgage lenders; up to 95% loan-to-value.
land_banking.source_title: Community Housing Capital website (loan products, home and team pages)
land_banking.note: Site totals (undated): $1.3 billion of capital deployed, $4.1 billion total development, 25,374 homes, 44 states. Leadership change: Cindy Holler, President and CEO, is retiring; Dana Chestnut, EVP/Chief Lending Officer, becomes President and CEO on 2027-01-01. Arif Rizvi is EVP/Chief Financial Officer. NeighborWorks America funds it with grants from its appropriation (described as an affiliated 'Capital Corporation' in the budget justification). Not a land banker and no lot-option structure.

financing.summary: First America Homes is a conventional for-sale builder, but it is a division of a private developer rather than a stand-alone company, and nothing about its debt, lenders or balance sheet is public. Its land comes two ways: lots developed by the parent's own Land division (for example 359 lots at Azalea District in Valley Ranch, where it is the exclusive builder), and finished homesites bought in other developers' communities in the 2026 expansion markets (81 lots at Leonard Trails in Anna, three Austin-area communities, nine San Antonio-area communities). The parent describes itself as well capitalized, cites $3.5B+ of assets under management and 25,000+ paper lots, and says it is buying positions from industry partners that want to shrink. No land banker, lot-option financier or lender is named anywhere public. It is a plausible land-banking customer, most likely at the parent level (funding the parent's lot development pipeline or the builder's fast growth toward a stated 5,000 homes a year by 2035), and the people to approach are the parent's CFO and Land division.
financing.land_strategy: Vertically integrated rather than land-light: the company's own framing is that First America Homes 'leverages in-house land development' from The Signorelli Company's integrated platform. In practice it is mixed: parent-developed lots in Houston-area master plans, plus finished-lot purchases from third-party developers in Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin and San Antonio. No owned-versus-optioned target is stated. The parent's land arm is also a lot seller: its 6,400-acre Austin Point lists nine outside builders and not First America Homes.

financing.summary: Private company with no SEC filings or rated debt, so lenders, facility terms, debt and lot counts are not public. What is visible is a self-development model: an in-house land arm (McBride Land Strategy) buys, entitles and develops large master plans, topped up with finished lots bought from other builders, builder joint ventures and public-private structures in which a city or county carries land or infrastructure cost. No land banker, lot-option financier or outside capital partner is named in any source opened, and no link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. The pipeline announced since 2025 is large relative to roughly 750 to 800 closings a year (854 lots at Havenwood, 700+ at the Jamestown Mall site, 587 in Rolla), which makes McBride a plausible land-banking prospect on paper, but there is no public sign that it uses third-party land capital today.
financing.land_strategy: Owns and develops its own land, in the company's framing a selective, margin-first approach. The CEO told Builder (Sept 2026, as relayed by STL.News) that McBride matches starts to demand, can cut starts because it is private, and follows a 'Next Exit' strategy of exurban sites near interstates chosen on job growth, access and land cost, with plans to grow beyond current volume over five to ten years. Land is sometimes bought through project-level entities (a 31.8-acre Union, MO purchase in Dec 2022 was made by St. Andrews Drive Development LLC, per the broker's release). No owned-versus-optioned target is stated.

financing.summary: Conventional for-sale builder that no longer finances itself: since 2026-10-07 its communities, lots and work in process sit on Century Communities' balance sheet, bought for about $160.2M of initial cash that Century drew on its $1.2B unsecured revolver (U.S. Bank agent, upsized and extended to November 2030 one week earlier). HistoryMaker's own pre-sale bank lines, lot counts and any land-bank arrangements were never public. The family model was integrated: sister company Jabez Development developed lots and HistoryMaker built on them; Jabez was not sold and keeps developing and delivering lots to Century under an ongoing contract, so the seller is now Century's lot developer in Dallas-Fort Worth. Century says it uses land banking only on a very limited basis and controls 45.1% of its 60,969 lots (2026-09-30, before HistoryMaker) through options, while its revolver balance rose from $51.5M to $456.0M in nine months and its stated priority is to hold debt to capital. Room for a land banker therefore sits in two places: Century's enlarged DFW lot pipeline (a parent-level conversation), and Jabez Development, a private developer that now carries horizontal risk for a public builder and has no disclosed capital partner.
financing.land_strategy: Before the sale: an integrated family platform, with Jabez Development (land acquisition, entitlement and development) feeding HistoryMaker Homes (for-sale) and ONM Living (build-to-rent); no owned/optioned split or target was ever published. After the sale: Century's strategy applies. Century describes its lots as 54.9% owned and 45.1% controlled at 2026-09-30, says it is moving toward lower-deposit lot contracts, and will take finished lots in DFW from Jabez Development on current and future communities.

land_banking.description: Sister land development company owned by the Mitchell family; not part of the sale. Historically the in-house lot developer for HistoryMaker Homes. Under the Century deal it completes land development on select (per the Q3 release, current and future) Century communities in Dallas-Fort Worth, and the two expect to pursue more DFW land together. Century's CEO called it an ongoing contractual relationship; the seller's adviser described the pattern as the seller continuing to sell finished lots to the acquirer.
land_banking.source_title: Century Communities press release 2026-10-08: Century Communities Triples Dallas-Fort Worth Footprint with Acquisition of HistoryMaker Homes
land_banking.note: No lot counts, takedown schedule, pricing, deposits or funding source for Jabez disclosed. Not a land banker: a private developer affiliated with the seller, and a possible land-bank customer or channel in its own right. 'Ongoing contractual relationship' is from the Q3 2026 call transcript (Motley Fool); the finished-lot comment is from HousingWire, 2026-10-08.

financing.summary: Esperanza Homes is the building arm of family-owned Rhodes Enterprises, which develops its own master-planned land and hands lots to its builder, so land is financed inside the family group rather than through options or a land banker. No land-bank, lot-option or outside equity partner is named in any source opened. Public records, as compiled by an aggregator, show the group borrowing from regional banks (International Bank of Commerce, Third Coast Bank, Bank OZK) through per-market Esperanza LLCs and development LLCs, including a $75M Third Coast Bank deed of trust recorded in late 2026. Tres Lagos infrastructure is partly reimbursed through a City of McAllen TIRZ and a public improvement district. It is a plausible but unproven land-banking customer: the growth plan (1,000 closings by 2027, new Laredo and Corpus Christi divisions, a 3,200-home Brownsville master plan) needs capital beyond the legacy family land, yet the group has so far chosen bank debt and self-development.
financing.land_strategy: Owns and develops most of its land through the parent. Rhodes Enterprises describes itself as vertically integrated: it master-plans and develops communities and Esperanza Homes builds in them. Stated holdings: Tres Lagos, McAllen (2,567 acres, 30-year plan, active); Bentsen Palm, Mission (2,600 acres, active since 2004); La Sienna, Edinburg (726 acres, 'now part of the Rhodes portfolio', about 350 acres undeveloped); Mirabella, Corpus Christi (about 300 acres, over 1,150 homes, active development); Estrella, Brownsville (proposed, over 3,200 homes). The family originally bought about 10,000 acres of Hidalgo County farmland. Outside the master plans it builds smaller stand-alone communities (Weslaco, San Juan, Mercedes, Harlingen, Brownsville, Laredo); whether those lots are self-developed or bought finished is not stated, and no owned-versus-optioned split is published.

land_banking.description: The parent is the land developer: it master-plans and develops Tres Lagos, Bentsen Palm, La Sienna, Mirabella and the proposed Estrella, and Esperanza Homes is the builder in them (Estrella and Mirabella pages say all homes are built by Esperanza). This in-house supply plays the role a land banker would otherwise play.

profile.summary: Not a conventional for-sale homebuilder: JCCG is a private, founder-owned build-to-rent (BTR) general contractor and lot developer in Atlanta that builds rental cottage, townhome and single-family communities for institutional investors, REITs and private developers, who own the finished communities. Its Builder 100 rank (No. 79) rests on 708 homes completed in 2025, plus 1,040 lots delivered, across GA, AL, FL and IN; it projects 1,150 completions in 2026 and 1,450 in 2027. It is the successor to Jim Chapman Communities, the founder's metro-Atlanta active-adult (55+) for-sale brand, and moved wholly to BTR in 2018. As a land-banking customer it is an edge case: it does source, entitle and develop land (it has a land acquisition team and lists 'you have land to sell' on its contact form), but the lots end up with rental owners rather than being taken down for sale, so any fit would be finished-lot or development funding for BTR projects, usually alongside the capital partner that owns the project.

financing.summary: Not a conventional for-sale homebuilder: JCCG is a private, founder-owned build-to-rent general contractor and lot developer, so most of the land and construction capital in its projects belongs to its clients, not to JCCG. Named or described capital sources are an unnamed publicly traded REIT (five communities), an unnamed publicly traded investment firm (which closed on the Dawsonville land together with JCCG in November 2024), a Trinitas Ventures / PCCP joint venture, NexMetro, AREY Group, BLDG Real Estate and a Scottsdale family office. Earlier (2021 to 2023) JCCG developed communities and sold them whole to institutional owners, including four communities of 971 homes closed in 2023. JCCG's own lenders, credit lines and balance sheet are not publicly disclosed, and no land banker or lot-option financier is named anywhere in its releases. For a land banker it is a weak direct customer (no for-sale takedown schedule, lots end up in rental ownership) but a possible channel: it delivered 1,040 finished lots in 2025, has a four-person land team, and its investor clients could use lot or development funding between land closing and vertical start.
financing.land_strategy: Capital-light by design. JCCG finds, entitles and develops sites and builds the homes, but under general-contractor or fee-build agreements for the investor or developer that owns the project; where JCCG originates the deal, the capital partner closes on the land with it. The company does not describe owned or optioned lot positions and states no land-light target.

The Cottages at Loxley, AL (250 homes, broke ground January 2026) is described as the fifth community with this REIT; Creekside Cottages, Opelika, AL (304 units) as the fourth; The Cottages at Villa Rica, GA (192 homes) was signed in August 2024.

financing.summary: Riverside is the homebuilding arm of Tim Fleet's Lackland Holdings, which buys and develops land in-house and sells finished lots to Riverside and to other builders, so the group already acts as its own land bank. Lackland's website says plainly that it is not interested in new financing sources and that it uses its own equity plus bank financing when necessary; it also holds income properties it says it never sells. Public-record listings point to Texas and regional banks (Simmons Bank, Vista Bank, Clayton Bank and Trust, American National Bank & Trust, Pinnacle, Vantage Bank Texas) lending to Riverside and to single-purpose Lackland land entities; no facility terms, lot counts or balance-sheet figures are public. This is a conventional for-sale builder (about 650 closings a year, DFW only) but a low-probability land-banking customer on its own stated terms; the realistic openings are selling it lots or a deal-by-deal partnership, which Lackland's site invites, and both run through Tim Fleet.
financing.land_strategy: Owns and self-develops. The affiliate Lackland Holdings acquires residentially zoned land, develops it (often into one-acre-plus homesites in exurban DFW counties) and sells lots to Riverside and to other builders; Riverside's in-house counsel described taking lots down from the development side through scheduled lot takedowns. No stated owned/optioned target and no third-party land banker. Lackland says it is 'always open' to buying more residential land or finished single-family lots.

land_banking.description: Tim Fleet's development company (formed 1991, same office as Riverside). It develops land and sells lots to multiple builders including what it calls 'our wholly owned Riverside Homebuilders', which makes it Riverside's captive lot supplier. Its site states it is not interested in new financing sources and funds itself with its own equity and bank financing when necessary.

profile.summary: Private Alabama production builder founded in 2006, headquartered in Opelika, building detached single-family homes (plus the entry-level THRIVE line) in about 20 cities across Auburn-Opelika, Montgomery, Huntsville, Dothan-Enterprise, Troy and the Columbus, Georgia area. It is a conventional for-sale builder that develops its own communities and buys raw land directly (it runs a public land-submissions page), financed by regional banks through a land affiliate, with no land banker named publicly, so it is a plausible but small land-banking prospect.

financing.summary: Stone Martin is a conventional for-sale homebuilder that funds itself privately: owner equity through a holding company (Sky Holdings, Inc.) and secured bank credit, with nothing rated, registered or disclosed. State lien records show its land affiliate, SMB Land, LLC, borrowing from Texas Capital Bank (since 2020, renewed in 2025) and from smaller regional lenders (Southern States Bank, BankPlus, Listerhill Credit Union), which points to a traditional buy-develop-and-own land model financed loan by loan. No land banker, lot-option partner, outside equity investor or joint-venture land partner is named in any public source opened, and no link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. For a land banker that means an open field but a small one: roughly 650 to 800 closings a year across secondary Alabama markets, with a CEO who personally came up through land.
financing.land_strategy: Appears to own and develop most of its land (inferred, not stated by the company). The company describes itself as building homes and developing its own communities, invites landowners to sell to it through a land-submissions page, and holds land in an affiliate (SMB Land, LLC) with bank liens. It has stated no land-light target and published no owned versus optioned split.

land_banking.description: Affiliated land-holding entity (formed May 2015, organizer Mitchell R. Martin, registered agent Frank Plan, same Opelika address as the builder). It is the borrower on the bank lien filings, so it appears to be where land is acquired, developed and financed before homes are built. This is an in-house structure, not a third-party land bank.

financing.summary: Veridian is a conventional for-sale homebuilder, privately held and family-owned inside Forgewell Building Group, with no SEC filings or rated or public debt found and no disclosed lender, facility, land banker, lot-option partner or joint venture. It is its own land developer: it buys raw land, entitles it and develops it in phases with an in-house land development team, releasing finished homesites to its own buyers a few dozen at a time. Its pipeline is concentrated in very large self-developed communities (Hill Valley 841 homesites, Reiland Grove 561, Midpoint Meadows about 250 lots, Arrowood 300), which ties up capital for years and makes it a plausible land-banking prospect on paper. Against that, nothing public shows it has ever used third-party lot capital, the founder is still chairman and principal owner, and the group is vertically integrated (trades, millwork, property management), so any approach would be to David Simon, Chris Ehlers and the finance head directly.
financing.land_strategy: Owns and self-develops (not land-light): the company describes itself as a neighborhood developer, buys raw farmland and entitles and develops it in phases; no stated option target and no public mention of lot-option or land-bank structures. Job-board search snippets (pages since removed, not opened) show it advertising a Director of Land Acquisition for Greater Milwaukee, which suggests it is adding land-buying capacity there.

financing.summary: Private, family- and employee-owned builder (Bright Industries family; ESOP since 2017) with no SEC filings and no public debt, so its credit lines, lenders and lot counts are not public. Its model is to buy developer-finished lots in third-party master-planned communities in DFW and on the Colorado Front Range (Hillwood, at Treeline, is the named developer partner), plus lots in the family's own Castle Hills (Bright Realty). financing.summary: Home Creations is a private, family-owned, conventional for-sale builder with no public debt, no SEC filings and no published lender, credit facility, land banker or capital partner. What is public points to a self-funded, owner-developer model in Oklahoma: land development is an in-house function, co-founder Jalal Farzaneh is reported as owner of Shaz Investments (a Norman land developer), and an engineering firm says Home Creations hired it to plan a 760-acre, roughly 2,000-unit community in Norman. In Houston, entered in 2022, its lot sources are not disclosed: the company names no developer for its Houston communities. A 2015 profile quoted a company executive saying the owners reinvest most earnings and that a shortage of developed lots was the main brake on growth. It is a plausible land-banking customer on two fronts (the large Norman tract and Houston lot supply), but there is no public sign that the family has used outside land capital.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed, with no stated owned-versus-optioned target. In Oklahoma the family entitles and develops much of its own land through affiliates and an in-house land development department, then builds it out. In Houston the lot source (own development or third-party developers) is not disclosed.

profile.summary: Private, founder-owned Oklahoma builder (founded 2000) that calls itself the state's largest: 633 closings in 2025 per the Builder 100, after a peak of 883 in 2021 per the company, selling from 29 listed communities, almost all around Oklahoma City, with a small Tulsa presence since 2022 and one community near Stillwater. It is a developer-builder: the owner buys and develops most of its own land through an affiliate rather than buying finished lots, and nine of the 29 communities are in 'coming soon' or 'grand opening' status, so new land is being brought on now.

financing.summary: Chesapeake Homes is a conventional for-sale builder: a private subsidiary of the Sandler family's L.M. Sandler & Sons, Inc. (Builder 100 rank 90; 631 closings and about $308M revenue in 2025). It has no public debt or SEC filings. Land comes mostly through a sister company, Wakefield Development, also owned by L.M. Sandler & Sons, which buys, entitles and develops lots across VA, NC, SC, MD, DE and GA, and has worked on other projects as a silent or side-by-side partner. The parent says it relies on 'long-standing banking and equity partnerships' and in-house capital, but no lender, facility or land banker is named publicly. A March 2026 posting for a Mid-Atlantic Land Acquisition Executive mentions options, joint ventures, takedowns, capital deployment with finance, and presentations to investment committees. That points to a growing, more structured land program, which makes it a plausible but unproven land-banking prospect. The likely contacts are Wakefield's project-finance/land lead, Clark Hetzler, and the owner Steve Sandler.
financing.land_strategy: Family vertical integration: the affiliated developer Wakefield Development acquires and develops land, and Chesapeake Homes builds on the finished lots. Wakefield's community list overlaps with Chesapeake communities such as River Club, Bridgewater, Coastal Club of the Carolinas, Traditions at Carolina Forest, Highgate and Ashville Park. No owned-versus-optioned framing or target is published. A 2026 land-acquisition job posting lists options, JVs and takedown structures among the deal types it handles.

financing.summary: ICI Homes is a private, family-owned company with no public debt, no SEC filings and no rating, so its lenders, facilities and balance sheet are not public. What is public is how it controls land: it develops its own communities in its Daytona Beach home market through special-purpose subsidiaries, it co-develops the 1,600-home Seven Pines community in Jacksonville in a partnership with David Weekley Homes that buys the land from the selling family in phases, and elsewhere it buys finished lots as a preferred builder from third-party master developers. No land banker, lot-option financier or outside capital partner is named in any source found, and there is no public link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon. It is a conventional for-sale builder and a plausible land-banking prospect on paper (it carries developer-scale land and a 2025 trade feature says it will add land to the south and on the Gulf coast), but the owner stresses long-horizon private ownership, so appetite for off-balance-sheet structures is untested.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed, leaning owner-developer. The company does not publish a land-light target. It self-develops large communities in Volusia and Flagler counties (Plantation Bay, Mosaic) and St. Johns County (the 572-acre Crossroads tract), shares land risk through a builder partnership with phased takedowns at Seven Pines, and takes finished lots from master developers such as The PARC Group (EverRange), Wellen Park, Sunbridge and IronCrest.

land_banking.description: Land seller with phased takedowns, which works like seller-side land banking: ICI Homes and David Weekley Homes hold rights to about 550-560 acres at Seven Pines in Jacksonville and buy it in three phases. The two builders announced the acquisition in Dec 2020 and expect to buy the final section in late 2026. The Daily Record says the staggered purchases spread out the acquisition cost.

financing.summary: Private, founder-led and self-described 'builder-owned' Florida builder (554 to 555 closings in 2025) with no public debt, no SEC filings and no disclosed lender, credit facility, land banker or outside capital partner. It is a conventional for-sale builder, but its land model is unusual: most homes go up one at a time on scattered infill lots it buys from individual owners and the MLS in pre-platted communities (Cape Coral, Lehigh Acres, Port Charlotte, Palm Bay, Citrus Springs, Marion Oaks), plus a build-on-your-lot programme, which needs little land capital and is a poor fit for a classic land-bank structure. The opening for a land banker is the newer community business: it took finished homesites in West Port (111 lots, 2022) and Babcock Ranch (291 homes, 2023), and in September 2026 was named one of five builders in Barron Collier's 2,000-home Brightshore in Naples, alongside Pulte, Toll, Taylor Morrison and M/I. So it is a plausible but small land-banking customer, most likely for bulk finished-lot takedowns in master plans; how it funds those today is not public.
financing.land_strategy: Asset-light by design rather than by option: the CEO has said the company enters markets where there is a single ('spot') lot opportunity because it carries much less risk, and the company's current land-acquisition job posting describes sourcing scattered, spot and infill lots from the MLS. It also solicits land sellers directly ('one or one-thousand lots') and takes finished homesites from master developers (West Port, Babcock Ranch, Brightshore). No owned/optioned split or stated target is published.

land_banking.description: Master developer of Brightshore (about 680 acres, roughly 2,000 homes, Immokalee Road, Naples). Christopher Alan Homes is one of five builders selected, with Toll Brothers, Taylor Morrison, Pulte and M/I Homes; its neighbourhood is marketed as Horizon at Brightshore. The developer says it will soon turn homesites over to builders, with models expected by summer 2027.

The builder's own site confirms the community as 'coming soon': https://christopheralanhomes.com/horizon-at-brightshore/. financing.summary: SJV Homes is a conventional private for-sale builder whose land and construction have been financed since 2013 through project joint ventures with one capital partner, Presidio Residential Capital of San Diego, which described itself in 2018 as funding 100 percent of SJV Homes' projects and operations and counted 40 joint communities and more than 5,000 homes by mid-2024. The joint venture buys land outright (raw or entitled parcels) and develops it; no land banker, lot-option provider, bank facility or note issue is publicly named for the builder itself, and nothing is filed publicly. Two things have changed in public view since 2024: Presidio has dropped out of the builder's press-release boilerplate (it still appeared in February 2024, not from February 2025 on), yet Presidio principal Paul Lucatuorto is listed as Co-CEO of SJV Homes on the October 2026 team page. Room for a land banker therefore depends on Presidio: it is either the incumbent to displace or, given its own committed capital was a stated $250M across 25-plus projects for all its builders, a partner that could use off-balance-sheet lot capital for a builder closing about 550 homes a year with four more neighborhoods coming from 2027.
financing.land_strategy: Owns through joint ventures rather than options: SJV Homes and Presidio Residential Capital close on land together (parcels sized for roughly 30 to 300 homes per community, per Presidio's Central Valley portfolio list, in Tulare, Kings, Kern and Fresno county towns) and develop and build it out in the venture. No stated owned/optioned target and no public mention of lot options or land banking. In February 2024 the company described a pipeline of nine new communities and expansions adding roughly 1,600 homes; in November 2026 it reported 19 active neighborhoods with four more scheduled (Keystone and Northgate in NW Visalia, Estrella and Mirabella in NW Hanford).

land_banking.description: Programmatic joint-venture equity partner since SJV Homes was formed in 2013: Presidio capitalises land purchase, development and build-out project by project. Presidio's June 2024 release counts 40 communities and more than 5,000 homes delivered through the partnership; this is JV ownership of the land, not a lot-option or land-bank structure.

profile.summary: Private entry-level, 100% spec builder founded in October 2021 by Wade Jurney (founder of Wade Jurney Homes, sold to Century Communities) with Michael Bergman and Gregg Erickson. financing.summary: National Home Corp. is a private, founder-owned entry-level builder (550 closings in 2025, pacing 800+ in 2026) that buys finished lots only, builds 100% spec and describes its land exposure as limited; it does not develop land and publishes no lot count. A conventional for-sale builder that also sells to and fee-builds for build-to-rent investors, it is a plausible but small land-banking customer: its stated plan to reach about 1,200 homes under construction by year-end 2026 and 1,500 to 1,800 closings in 2027 implies a much larger finished-lot pipeline than it has needed so far, and its site openly solicits developed homesites from sellers. No land banker, lot-option financier, equity sponsor or credit facility is publicly named; the only lender names on record are from 2022 (Wells Fargo, 'Regents' as printed, Fifth Third and Flagstar funding start-up operations). The one disclosed joint venture is NHC Mortgage with loanDepot, a buyer-mortgage venture, not land capital. No public link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found.
financing.land_strategy: Land-light by design: buys finished lots from developers, builds standardized plans 100% spec, and aims to keep capital exposed for as short a time as possible (the Wade Jurney Homes playbook: just-in-time lot takedowns, fast inventory turns, pace over margin). No stated owned/optioned target. The company site runs a 'We Buy Lots' / 'Sell Land' page asking owners of developed homesites and build-for-rent partners to submit deals.

financing.summary: Colina Homes is a conventional for-sale builder, privately owned by its founder, with no public debt, no SEC filings and no published lender, lot count or capital partner. profile.summary: Private, founder-owned semi-custom builder based in Rehoboth Beach, DE, founded in 2003 by Chris Schell; a conventional for-sale builder at the upper end of the price range, with four divisions (Delaware, Richmond, Nashville, Boise since 2024) and about 45 communities on its site. Its home-market lots are largely developed by the family's affiliated developer, Ocean Atlantic Companies, which raises outside investor equity; the three newer divisions buy developer lots and contract raw land, and have no public land-banking partner, so they are the natural opening for a land banker.

financing.summary: Schell Brothers is a private, founder-controlled, conventional for-sale builder with no public debt, no ratings and no SEC filings found, so its bank lines and balance sheet are not public. What is public is the land model. In its Delaware home market, lots are largely developed by the Schell family's affiliated developer, Ocean Atlantic Companies (run by Chris Schell's twin brother Preston), which funds each project with outside investor equity alongside its own and has used institutional land capital before (a 2012 joint venture with Mountain Real Estate Capital). In Richmond, Nashville and Boise there is no affiliate: Schell buys lots that developers such as HHHunt build for it, contracts raw land subject to rezoning, and co-develops larger sites with another builder (Main Street Homes). No land banker, lot-option financier or link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. It is a plausible land-banking customer, mainly for the three expansion divisions and for large self-assembled sites such as the 76-acre Westford Glen; in Delaware the affiliate and its investor base already fill that role, so the pitch there is to Ocean Atlantic as much as to Schell.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed, with no stated owned-versus-optioned target. Delaware: lots come largely from the affiliated developer Ocean Atlantic Companies, which develops communities with investor equity and hands the home building to Schell Brothers. Richmond, Nashville, Boise: finished lots from third-party and master-plan developers, plus raw land put under contract and taken through rezoning by Schell's own division land directors. Pro Builder (Dec 2023) described large land holdings around Rehoboth Beach built up since the 2007-08 downturn.

land_banking.description: Schell family development group in Rehoboth Beach (founded 1997 by Preston Schell and Gene Lankford) that develops residential communities in Delaware and hands home building to Schell Brothers. Its lot-development page lists Walden (265 units, 159 acres, Lewes area) and Marlin Chase (75 homes, Ocean View) and links both to schellbrothers.com; it also lists Brighton (674 lots, Middletown) as a future project. It functions as Schell Brothers' in-house land developer and off-balance-sheet lot source in Delaware.
land_banking.source_title: Ocean Atlantic Companies: Residential Lot Development (company site)
land_banking.note: Ocean Atlantic's investor page says it takes outside investors into each deal, pays preferred returns during development and puts in significant equity of its own; its about page (undated) cites 2,000 home sites in the pipeline. Preston Schell's bio lists Schell Brothers among the group's companies and says he is managing member of about 50 project LLCs. Ocean Atlantic also sells to other builders: D.R. Horton is building its 289-home Woodfield Preserve in Milton. A Dec 2025 job advert for an Ocean Atlantic Director of Site Development (career.com, Rehoboth Beach) described Ocean Atlantic as a member of the Schell Brothers family of companies, so the tie is current. Lot counts specific to Schell Brothers, takedown terms and the investors' names are not public.

land_banking.description: Richmond BizSense reported that HHHunt is developing the home lots for Schell Brothers in the 669-unit, roughly 250-acre Bethia Road project in Chesterfield County (307 single-family homes and 74 townhomes for Schell; HHHunt builds the 288 apartments). Site work had started by June 2024.
